# Dirichlet's theorem, conditional on `L(1, χ) ≠ 0`

This file assembles the pieces into the reduction that Dirichlet himself made in 1837:

> *If `L(1, χ) ≠ 0` for every non-principal character `χ` modulo `q`, then for every `a` coprime
> to `q` there are infinitely many primes `p ≡ a (mod q)`.*

Indeed, by the sieve, `φ(q) · Σ_{n ≤ N, n ≡ a} Λ(n)/n = Σ_χ conj χ(a) S_χ(N)`. The principal
character contributes at least `log N − 1 − 2q` (Mertens), and each of the other characters a
bounded amount (since `L(1, χ) ≠ 0`, file `ChebyshevSums`). So `Σ_{n ≤ N, n ≡ a} Λ(n)/n → ∞`.
If there were only finitely many primes `p ≡ a`, all below `N₀`, this sum would be at most
`N₀ + 4`: the primes contribute `log p / p ≤ 1` each, and the higher prime powers at most `4`
(file `PrimePowers`). This contradiction proves the theorem — given the non-vanishing, which is
the subject of the next files.

# The Möbius function

The **Möbius function** (Möbius 1832; the notation `μ` is Mertens') is `μ(n) = (−1)^k` if `n` is
a product of `k` distinct primes, and `μ(n) = 0` if some square of a prime divides `n`. It is
the inverse of the constant function `1` for Dirichlet convolution:

  `Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) = 1` if `n = 1`, and `0` if `n > 1`,

which is the inclusion–exclusion principle in arithmetic form. Combined with
`Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n` it gives the inverse relation `Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) log d = −Λ(n)`. Both are
proved by peeling off one prime: the divisors of `pᵃ m` (`p ∤ m`) are the `pⁱ e` with `e ∣ m`,
and only `i = 0, 1` contribute, with `μ(p e) = −μ(e)`.

These identities let us *invert* `L(1, χ)` in the next file: they are the elementary shadow of
`1/L(s, χ) = Σ μ(n) χ(n) n⁻ˢ` and `−L'/L(s, χ) = Σ Λ(n) χ(n) n⁻ˢ`.

# `L(1, χ) ≠ 0` for characters that are not real

Suppose `L(1, χ) = 0` for a non-principal character. Inverting `L(1, χ)` with the Möbius
function shows that then the twisted Chebyshev sum is *large and negative*:

  `S_χ(N) = −log N + O(1)`.

Indeed `Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) log (N/d) = log N · [n = 1] + Λ(n)`, so summing against `χ(n)/n` gives

  `log N + S_χ(N) = Σ_{d ≤ N} μ(d) χ(d) log(N/d) / d · Σ_{m ≤ N/d} χ(m)/m`,

and if `L(1, χ) = 0` each inner sum is a tail of the series, of size `≤ 2qd/N`; the total is at
most `(2q/N) Σ_{d ≤ N} log (N/d) = (2q/N)(N log N − log N!) ≤ 2q`.

Now if `χ` is **not real**, then `χ̄ ≠ χ` and `L(1, χ̄) = conj L(1, χ) = 0` as well. But the sum of
all the `S_ψ(N)` over the characters is `φ(q) Σ_{n ≡ 1} Λ(n)/n ≥ 0`, while the principal character
contributes at most `log N + O(1)`, the two characters `χ, χ̄` contribute `−2 log N + O(1)`, and
every other character `O(1)` or less. For large `N` the total would be negative — a contradiction.
So a vanishing `L(1, χ)` can only come from a *real* character; that case needs a different idea
(next file).

# Real characters: the divisor sums `r(n) = Σ_{d ∣ n} χ(n)` and the sum `Σ r(n)/√n`

For a **real** character `χ` (values `0, ±1`) the argument used for complex characters breaks
down: `χ̄ = χ`, so a zero of `L(1, χ)` would be counted only once. The classical way out
(Mertens 1897, simplified by many since) looks at the divisor sums

  `r(n) = Σ_{d ∣ n} χ(d)`.

Because `χ` is completely multiplicative, `r(pᵃ m) = (1 + χ(p) + ⋯ + χ(p)ᵃ) · r(m)` for `p ∤ m`;
with `χ(p) ∈ {−1, 0, 1}` each factor is `≥ 0`, and `≥ 1` when `a` is even. Hence

  `r(n) ≥ 0` for all `n`, and `r(k²) ≥ 1`.

(In modern terms, `ζ(s) L(s, χ)` is the zeta function of a quadratic field and has non-negative
coefficients.) Consequently the sum `T(N) = Σ_{n ≤ N} r(n)/√n` grows at least like
`Σ_{k ≤ √N} 1/k ≥ log √N`. On the other hand, counting the pairs `(d, m)` with `dm ≤ N`,

  `T(N) = Σ_{d ≤ N} χ(d)/√d · U(N/d)`,   `U(K) = Σ_{1 ≤ m ≤ K} 1/√m`,

which the next file shows to be `2√N · L(1, χ) + O(1)`. So `L(1, χ) = 0` is impossible.

where `V(K)` is non-increasing with values in `[−2, 0]` (compare the sum with `∫ dt/√t`):

* the **tail** `d > M` is a sum of `χ(d)` against the non-increasing weights `U(N/d)/√d`, so by

So `T(M²)` stays bounded, while `T(M²) ≥ log (M + 1)` because `r(n) ≥ 0` and `r(k²) ≥ 1`. This

# Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions

> **Theorem (Dirichlet, 1837).** If `a` and `q ≥ 1` are coprime, there are infinitely many
> primes `p ≡ a (mod q)`.

Euclid's argument gives infinitely many primes; variants of it (file `PrimesMod4`) handle a few
progressions such as `4k + 1` and `4k + 3`, but no purely algebraic trick is known that works for
every progression. Dirichlet's proof was the first to bring analysis — infinite series, limits,
and the group characters of `(ℤ/qℤ)ˣ` — to bear on a question about whole numbers, and it is
usually counted as the birth of **analytic number theory**. He was inspired by Euler's proof
(1737) that `Σ 1/p` diverges, which is the case `q = 1`. Our `mertens_lower`,
`Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)/n ≥ log N − 1`, is the case `q = 1` of Dirichlet's theorem in Mertens' form;
it gives the divergence of `Σ log p / p`, which is weaker than Euler's `Σ 1/p = ∞`.

The proof formalised in this part follows the elementary route through the values `L(1, χ)`:

1. `Characters`, `DualGroup`, `DirichletCharacters` — characters of finite abelian groups,
   orthogonality, Dirichlet characters and the sieve for one residue class;
2. `ArithmeticFunctions`, `Mertens`, `PrimePowers` — divisor sums, the von Mangoldt function,
   Chebyshev's bound and Mertens' estimate;
3. `LFunction` — convergence of `L(1, χ) = Σ χ(n)/n` by Abel summation;
4. `ChebyshevSums`, `DirichletConditional` — the key identity, and the reduction of the theorem
   to `L(1, χ) ≠ 0`;

# Toward the prime number theorem I: finite sums and logarithms

The **prime number theorem** says that the number `π(x)` of primes up to `x` is asymptotic to
`x / log x`: the ratio `π(x) log x / x` tends to `1`. Gauss, as a teenager in 1792, noticed in
tables of primes that their density near `x` is about `1 / log x`; Legendre (1798, 1808) proposed
the similar formula `x / (log x − 1.08366)`. Chebyshev (1852) proved by elementary means that the
ratio stays between two positive constants (see `Chebyshev`), and Riemann's memoir of 1859
showed that the finer question is governed by the complex zeros of the zeta function. The
theorem was proved in 1896, independently by **Hadamard** and **de la Vallée Poussin**, using the
theory of functions of a complex variable — above all the fact that `ζ(s)` has no zeros on the
line `Re s = 1`.

For half a century it was believed that no proof could avoid complex analysis: the theorem
seemed to "know" about the zeros of `ζ`. In 1948 **Atle Selberg** found an elementary
"symmetry formula", and **Paul Erdős** and Selberg then derived the prime number theorem from it
without any complex analysis (Selberg's own paper and the joint use of Erdős's ideas led to a
well-known priority dispute; both published proofs in 1949, and Selberg's Fields Medal of 1950
cited this work). "Elementary" here does not mean easy — it means using only real numbers,
limits and the logarithm. Philosophically the result was a lesson about *purity of method*:
what a theorem is "about" does not dictate which tools are needed to prove it, and an apparently
deep dependence on one branch of mathematics can turn out to be an artefact of the first proof.

The files `PNT*` follow the elementary route as far as it goes in this development. This first
file only gathers tools: identities for finite sums `Σ_{k<n} a(k)` (exchanging a double sum,
picking out a single term, counting multiples), and inequalities for the logarithm
(`log y ≤ y − 1`, and the crude Stirling-type bounds `n log n − n ≤ log n! ≤ n log n`).

# Toward the prime number theorem II: Chebyshev's functions θ and ψ

Counting primes one by one, as `π(x)` does, turns out to be awkward. Chebyshev's insight (1850s)
was to *weight* each prime by its logarithm:

* `θ(x) = Σ_{p ≤ x} log p` — the logarithm of the primorial `x#`;
* `ψ(x) = Σ_{pᵏ ≤ x, k ≥ 1} log p` — the same, but every prime power `pᵏ` also counts, with
  weight `log p`.

The second is the more natural: `ψ(x) = Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n)`, where **von Mangoldt's function**
`Λ(n)` is `log p` if `n` is a power of the prime `p` and `0` otherwise. The point of the
weighting is that `Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n` — unique factorisation, written additively — so that
`log n! = Σ_{d ≤ n} Λ(d) ⌊n/d⌋`, the identity driving the next files. The prime number theorem
becomes the statement `ψ(x) ∼ x`: the primes, weighted by their logarithms, have density one.

In this file (for natural numbers `N`):

* `Λ`, `θ`, `ψ`, and the identity `ψ(N) = Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)`;
* `θ(N) ≤ ψ(N) ≤ π(N) · log N ≤ N · log 1024`, and `θ(N) ≤ N · log 4` from Erdős's primorial
  bound — so θ and ψ are `O(N)`;
* `ψ(N) − θ(N) ≤ √N · log N`: higher prime powers are rare, since only primes `p ≤ √N` have a
  square below `N`.

Sums over prime powers are written as double sums over pairs `(p, k)`; for a prime `p` the
number of exponents `k ≥ 1` with `pᵏ ≤ N` is `ppCount p N`, the integer part of
`log N / log p`.

# Toward the prime number theorem III: three equivalent forms

The prime number theorem can be stated in three ways, and this file proves that they are
equivalent:

  `π(N) · log N / N → 1`   ⇔   `θ(N) / N → 1`   ⇔   `ψ(N) / N → 1`.

The first is Gauss's and Legendre's conjecture — the primes up to `N` number about `N / log N`.
The last is the form in which the theorem is actually *proved*, both in the complex-analytic
proofs of Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin (1896) and in the elementary proof of Selberg and
Erdős (1949): `ψ` is the function that interacts well with multiplication, through
`Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n`.

* `ψ ↔ θ`: the difference `ψ(N) − θ(N) ≤ √N · log N` (previous file) is `o(N)`, because
  `log N` grows more slowly than any power of `N` — here we only need `log m ≤ 2√m`.
* `θ ↔ π`: trivially `θ(N) ≤ π(N) log N`. Conversely, cutting at `M = ⌊N/k⌋`, the primes in
  `(M, N]` each contribute at least `log M ≥ log N − log 2k`, and there are at most
  `π(M) ≤ M log 1024 / log M` primes below `M` (Chebyshev). So
  `π(N) log N − θ(N) ≤ (log 1024 / k) · N + π(N) log 2k`, and the right side is at most `εN`
  once `k` is large and then `N` is large (since `π(N) ≤ N log 1024 / log N` and
  `log N → ∞`). This replaces the usual partial summation `π(x) = θ(x)/log x + ∫ θ(t)/(t log² t)`.

The statements are about sequences indexed by natural numbers `N`, with limits in the sense of
Part II (`Tendsto`).

# Toward the prime number theorem IV: Mertens' theorems

Franz **Mertens** proved in 1874, by elementary means, that the primes are distributed "on
average" exactly as the prime number theorem predicts, when weighted by `1/p`:

  `Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)/n = log N + O(1)`   and   `Σ_{p ≤ N} log p / p = log N + O(1)`.

These are much weaker than `ψ(N) ∼ N` (they would follow from it by partial summation, but not
conversely), yet they are the foundation of every elementary approach, including Selberg's.

The proof rests on one identity and one estimate.

* **The identity** `log N! = Σ_{pᵏ ≤ N} ⌊N/pᵏ⌋ · log p`, i.e. `log N! = Σ_{d ≤ N} Λ(d) ⌊N/d⌋`.
  It combines unique factorisation in additive form, `log m = Σ_p vₚ(m) log p`, with
  **Legendre's formula** `vₚ(N!) = Σ_k ⌊N/pᵏ⌋` from the `Binomial` file.
* **The estimate** `N log N − N ≤ log N! ≤ N log N` (a crude form of Stirling's formula, from
  `N! ≤ Nᴺ` and `Nᴺ/N! ≤ eᴺ`).

Replacing `⌊N/d⌋` by `N/d` costs at most `Σ_{d ≤ N} Λ(d) = ψ(N) ≤ N log 1024` (previous files).
Dividing by `N`: `−1 ≤ Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n)/n − log N ≤ log 1024`.

For the second theorem one removes the higher prime powers: their contribution
`Σ_p Σ_{k ≥ 2} log p / pᵏ ≤ Σ_p log p / (p(p−1))` is bounded by `2`, by comparison with the
telescoping sum of `(2 + log n)/n`.

# Toward the prime number theorem V: the Möbius function and divisor sums

Selberg's formula needs one more classical tool: **Möbius inversion** (Möbius, 1832; the
function `μ` already appears implicitly in Euler). The **Möbius function** is

  `μ(n) = (−1)ᵏ` if `n` is a product of `k` distinct primes, and `μ(n) = 0` if `p² ∣ n` for
  some prime `p`.

Its defining property is `Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) = [n = 1]`: summing `μ` over the divisors of any
`n > 1` gives zero, because the divisors with and without a given prime `p` cancel in pairs
`d ↔ p d`. This makes `μ` the inverse of the constant function `1` under *Dirichlet convolution*
`(f ∗ g)(n) = Σ_{d ∣ n} f(d) g(n/d)`, so that `F = f ∗ 1` can be solved for `f = F ∗ μ`.

Applied to `log = Λ ∗ 1` (unique factorisation: `Σ_{d ∣ n} Λ(d) = log n`), inversion gives

  `Λ(n) = Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) log(n/d) = −Σ_{d ∣ n} μ(d) log d`,

the identity that will feed the Tatuzawa–Iseki form of Selberg's argument.

We define `μ(n)` as a product of local factors `∏_{q ≤ n prime} m_q(n)` with `m_q(n) = 1, −1, 0`
according as `v_q(n) = 0, 1, ≥ 2`; then `μ(pm) = −μ(m)` for `p ∤ m` and `μ(pm) = 0` for `p ∣ m`
are factor-by-factor computations with the valuations of the `Binomial` file.

# Toward the prime number theorem VI: the Tatuzawa–Iseki identity

Selberg's own derivation of his formula (1949) inverted the function `Λ(n) log n + (Λ ∗ Λ)(n)`
with the Möbius function directly. A tidier route, due to **Tatuzawa and Iseki** (1951), packages
the inversion once and for all in an identity about arbitrary functions: if

  `G(x) = log x · Σ_{n ≤ x} F(x/n)`,

then

  `F(x) log x + Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n) F(x/n) = Σ_{d ≤ x} μ(d) G(x/d)`.

The left side is "Selberg-shaped"; the right side is a Möbius average of `G`. One applies it to
two functions `F₁ = ψ` and `F₂(x) = x − c` whose `G`'s nearly agree, so that the difference of the
right sides is small, and reads off the asymptotics of the left side.

We prove the identity for an integer `x = N`, with the values `F(N/n)` given as an arbitrary
sequence `Φ(n)` (this covers both `ψ(⌊N/n⌋)` and `N/n − c`): with
`Γ(d) = log(N/d) · Σ_{n ≤ N/d} Φ(dn)` (here `Φ(dn)` plays the role of `F(x/(dn))`),

  `Σ_{d ≤ N} μ(d) Γ(d) = Φ(1) log N + Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) Φ(n)`.

The proof reorganises the double sum over `d·n ≤ N` as a sum over `m = dn` and its divisors
(the **hyperbola reindexing**), and then uses `Σ_{d ∣ m} μ(d) = [m = 1]` and
`Σ_{d ∣ m} μ(d) log d = −Λ(m)` from the previous file.

# Toward the prime number theorem VII: estimates for Selberg's formula

To apply the Tatuzawa–Iseki identity we need three classical estimates, each sharper than the
crude bounds used for Mertens' theorems:

* **Euler's constant.** `H(M) = 1 + 1/2 + ⋯ + 1/M = log M + γ + O(1/M)`. The sequence
  `H(M) − log M` decreases, `H(M) − log(M+1)` increases, and they differ by
  `log(1 + 1/M) ≤ 1/M`; so both converge to a common limit `γ` (Euler 1734; `γ ≈ 0.5772`) and
  `0 ≤ H(M) − log M − γ ≤ 1/M`. Whether `γ` is irrational is still unknown.
* **Stirling with a bounded error.** `log M! = M log M − M + ½ log M + O(1)`, here taken from the
  Stirling file of Part VIII (the sequence `log M! + M − (M + ½) log M` decreases from `1` and
  stays above `3/4`).
* **A logarithmic average.** `Σ_{d ≤ N} log²(N/d) ≤ 6N`: the sum is a Riemann sum for
  `∫₀ᴺ log²(N/t) dt = 2N`; we compare term by term with `h(t) = t (log²(N/t) + 2 log(N/t) + 2)`,
  whose derivative is `log²(N/t)`, by the mean value theorem.

We also record **Chebyshev's identity** `Σ_{n ≤ M} ψ(M/n) = log M!`, the form of
`log M! = Σ Λ(d) ⌊M/d⌋` that the Tatuzawa–Iseki identity consumes.

# Toward the prime number theorem VIII: Selberg's symmetry formula

In the spring of 1948 Atle Selberg, then at the Institute for Advanced Study, proved the asymptotic
formula

  `ψ(x) log x + Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n) ψ(x/n) = 2x log x + O(x)`,

equivalently `Σ_{p ≤ x} log² p + Σ_{pq ≤ x} log p log q = 2x log x + O(x)`. It is called a
*symmetry* formula because it weighs a prime `p` and the products `pq` symmetrically; heuristically
it says that the primes and the products of two primes together have exactly the density
`2 log x` they would have if `ψ(x) ∼ x`. Unlike `ψ(x) ∼ x` itself, it can be proved by
manipulating finite sums — and from it the prime number theorem follows by a delicate but purely
real-variable ("tauberian") argument. Erdős, learning of the formula, used it to prove that
`p_{n+1}/p_n → 1`; Selberg then completed a proof of the prime number theorem, and both published
elementary proofs in 1949 (Selberg in the *Annals of Mathematics*, Erdős in the *Proceedings of
the National Academy of Sciences*). How much each owed to the other became a bitter dispute,
documented in letters of the time; Selberg's Fields Medal (1950) cited this work, and Erdős
received the Cole Prize (1951) for his paper. We take no side.

Our proof follows the Tatuzawa–Iseki route (previous files). Apply the identity
`Σ_{d ≤ N} μ(d) Γ(d) = Φ(1) log N + Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) Φ(n)` to

  `Φ(k) = ψ(⌊N/k⌋) − (N/k − c)`, with `c = γ + 1`.

On the right this gives `ψ(N) log N + Σ Λ(n) ψ(N/n)` minus
`(N − c) log N + N Σ Λ(n)/n − c ψ(N) = 2N log N + O(N)` (Mertens). On the left, with
`M = ⌊N/d⌋` and `y = N/d`, Chebyshev's identity gives
`Σ_{n ≤ M} Φ(dn) = log M! − y H(M) + cM`, and Stirling plus Euler's constant show this is
`O(log y)`; so `|Γ(d)| ≤ 4 log²(N/d) + 3`, and the logarithmic average
`Σ_{d ≤ N} log²(N/d) ≤ 6N` makes the whole left side `O(N)`.

# Toward the prime number theorem IX: Selberg's formula with `Λ ∗ Λ`

Selberg's formula is usually quoted in the form

  `Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n) log n + Σ_{mn ≤ x} Λ(m) Λ(n) = 2x log x + O(x)`,

in which the two kinds of "almost primes" — prime powers weighted by `log² p`, and products of
two prime powers weighted by `log p log q` — appear side by side. Writing
`(Λ ∗ Λ)(k) = Σ_{d ∣ k} Λ(d) Λ(k/d)` for the Dirichlet convolution, this file derives that form
from the `ψ`-form of the previous file. Two small steps are needed:

* `Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) ψ(N/n) = Σ_{k ≤ N} (Λ ∗ Λ)(k)` — the hyperbola reindexing again;
* `0 ≤ ψ(N) log N − Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) log n ≤ N log 1024` — by Abel summation the difference is
  `Σ_{j < N} ψ(j) (log(j+1) − log j)`, and each term is at most `j log 1024 · (1/j)`.

## From here to the prime number theorem

The prime number theorem `ψ(N)/N → 1` follows from Selberg's formula by the Erdős–Selberg
*tauberian* argument (in outline after Levinson's "motivated account", 1969). It is formalised in
the files that follow, using finite sums in place of integrals: `PNTRemainder` (Selberg's formula
for `R(N) = ψ(N) − N`), `PNTIterated` (`|R(N)| log² N ≤ Σ a(k) |R(N/k)| + O(N log N)`),
`PNTTauberianA`–`C` (sign changes, averaging, and the improvement lemma), and `PNTTheorem`
(`prime_number_theorem`). For comparison, the Isabelle formalisation of this proof by Avigad,
Donnelly, Gray and Raff (2007) ran to about 30 000 lines.

# Toward the prime number theorem X: the remainder `R(N) = ψ(N) − N`

The prime number theorem says that the **remainder** `R(N) = ψ(N) − N` is `o(N)`. This file
rewrites Selberg's formula in terms of `R` and collects the auxiliary facts about `R` that the
Erdős–Selberg tauberian argument (next files) needs:

* **Selberg's formula for the remainder**:
  `R(N) log N + Σ_{n ≤ N} Λ(n) R(⌊N/n⌋) = O(N)` — the main terms `2N log N` cancel exactly
  against `N log N + Σ Λ(n) ⌊N/n⌋ = N log N + log N!`;
* the **Selberg weights** `a(k) = Λ(k) log k + (Λ ∗ Λ)(k) ≥ 0`, with summatory function
  `A(N) = 2N log N + O(N)`, and the logarithmic average `Σ_{k ≤ N} a(k)/k ≤ log² N + O(log N)`
  (by Abel summation and `Σ log j / j ≤ ½ log² N + ½`);
* a **short-interval bound** `(ψ(n) − ψ(m)) log m ≤ 2(n − m)(log n + 1) + O(n)`: primes cannot
  crowd into an interval more than twice as densely as expected (another consequence of Selberg's
  formula, since `a(k) ≥ Λ(k) log k`);
* the **mean value** `|Σ_{n ≤ N} R(n)/(n(n+1))| ≤ B`: on average `R` is neither positive nor
  negative, which will force it to change sign in every long multiplicative interval.

# Toward the prime number theorem XI: Selberg's formula iterated

Selberg's formula for the remainder, `R(x) log x + Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n) R(x/n) = O(x)`, expresses
`R(x)` through the values `R(x/n)` — but with the weights `Λ(n)`, whose total `ψ(x)` is the
unknown itself. The trick of the Erdős–Selberg argument is to apply the formula a second time,
to each `R(x/m)`, and combine:

  `R(x) log² x = −Σ_{k ≤ x} Λ(k) log k · R(x/k) + Σ_{k ≤ x} (Λ ∗ Λ)(k) R(x/k) + O(x log x)`.

Taking absolute values,

  `|R(x)| log² x ≤ Σ_{k ≤ x} a(k) |R(x/k)| + O(x log x)`,   `a(k) = Λ(k) log k + (Λ ∗ Λ)(k)`,

and now the weights `a(k)` are *known* on average: `Σ_{k ≤ y} a(k) = 2y log y + O(y)` is
Selberg's formula once more. After division by `x`, `|R(x)|/x` is bounded by a weighted average
of the values `|R(y)|/y` at `y = x/k`, with weights `a(k)/k` of total `log² x + O(log x)`. The
next files show that this average is strictly smaller than the largest value, unless that value
is `0`.

The proof is a bookkeeping exercise: multiply Selberg's formula at `N` by `log N`, subtract the
formula at each `⌊N/m⌋` weighted by `Λ(m)`, recognise the double sum
`Σ_m Λ(m) Σ_n Λ(n) R(⌊N/(mn)⌋)` as `Σ_k (Λ ∗ Λ)(k) R(⌊N/k⌋)` (hyperbola reindexing), and
control the rounding `log N − log ⌊N/m⌋ = log m + O(1/⌊N/m⌋)`.

# Toward the prime number theorem XII: where the remainder is small

Write `V(n) = R(n)/n = ψ(n)/n − 1`; the prime number theorem says `V(n) → 0`. The tauberian
argument needs to know that `V` is small on *many* `n` — enough of them, measured
logarithmically, to pull the weighted average of the previous file strictly below its maximum.
This file proves the decisive qualitative fact:

  for every `ε > 0` there are `K` and `T` such that every interval `(y, Ky]` with `y` large
  contains an `m` with `|V(n)| ≤ ε/2` for **all** `n ∈ [m, m + m/T]`.

Three ingredients combine:

* **`V` changes sign.** The mean value `|Σ_{n ≤ N} R(n)/(n(n+1))| ≤ B` (in the form
  `Σ V(n)/(n+1)`) forbids `V > ε/4` throughout `(y, Ky]` once `log K` is large, because
  `Σ_{y < n ≤ Ky} 1/(n+1) ≈ log K`; likewise `V < −ε/4` is forbidden.
* **`V` moves in small steps.** `V(n+1) − V(n) = (Λ(n+1) − 1 − V(n))/(n+1)` is `O(log n / n)`,
  so a discrete intermediate value argument finds `m` with `|V(m)| ≤ ε/4`.
* **`V` is almost Lipschitz on the logarithmic scale.** By the short-interval bound,
  `|V(n) − V(m)| ≤ (5 + C₀)(n − m)/n + 2 KA / log m` for `m ≤ n ≤ 2m`; so `V` stays below `ε/2`
  on `[m, m + m/T]` when `T` is large.

This is the elementary substitute for the observation, in the analytic proofs, that `ζ` has no
zero on the line `Re s = 1`: the primes cannot conspire to keep `ψ(x)/x` away from `1` for long
stretches.

# The prime number theorem

This file completes the Erdős–Selberg proof. The engine is an **improvement lemma**:

  if `|V(n)| ≤ α` for all large `n`, where `ε ≤ α ≤ C₀`, then `|V(n)| ≤ α − δ` for all large `n`,

with `δ = δ(ε) > 0` independent of `α`. Iterating it finitely often brings the bound below any
`ε`, so `V(n) = ψ(n)/n − 1 → 0`: **`ψ(N) ∼ N`**, which by the equivalences of
`PNTEquivalence` is the prime number theorem `π(N) ∼ N / log N`.

The proof of the improvement lemma is the weighted-average argument. In

  `|V(N)| log² N ≤ Σ_{k ≤ N} (a(k)/k) |V(⌊N/k⌋)| + O(log N)`

every term has `|V(⌊N/k⌋)| ≤ α` except for `k > N/Y₀` (a tail of weight `O(log N)`). Choose
good intervals `[m_j, m_j + m_j/T]` (where `|V| ≤ ε/2`) inside the multiplicatively spaced
ranges `(Y_j, K Y_j]`, `Y_j = Y₀ (2K)^j`; for `j < J ≈ log N / (2 log 2K)` the corresponding
ranges of `k` are disjoint and each carries weight `≥ (log N)/(8T) − O(1)`. So a proportion
`≈ 1/(16 T log 2K)` of the total weight `log² N` sits on values `≤ ε/2 ≤ α − ε/2`, and the
average drops by about `ε/(32 T log 2K)`; after allowing for the error terms we take
`δ = ε/(32 T log (2K)²) = ε/(64 T log 2K)`.

## Historical note

This is, in substance, the argument of Selberg's 1949 paper, streamlined in the manner of
Levinson's "motivated account" (1969) and of the treatment in Hardy and Wright (ch. XXII).
It is elementary in the technical sense — no complex numbers, no Fourier analysis, no zeta
function — but it is not short: in this development it rests on fifteen files and some
5 000 lines, from Chebyshev's functions through Mertens' theorems, Möbius inversion, the
Tatuzawa–Iseki identity, Euler's constant and Stirling's formula to Selberg's formula and its
iteration. Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin needed the zeros of `ζ(s)`; Erdős and Selberg showed
that the theorem is, after all, a statement about finite sums of logarithms.

# The prime number theorem

  **`π(N) ∼ N / log N`**: the number of primes up to `N`, multiplied by `log N / N`, tends to `1`.

Gauss guessed it from tables at fifteen (1792); Legendre proposed a version in 1798. Chebyshev
(1852) showed that `π(N) log N / N` stays between two constants, and Riemann (1859) tied the
question to the zeros of the zeta function. Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin proved it in 1896
by complex analysis. Selberg and Erdős gave the first *elementary* proof in 1948/49, and that
is the proof formalised in the files `PNT*` of this part, ending here.

The last step only iterates the improvement lemma. Chebyshev's bound gives `|V(n)| ≤ C₀`
everywhere, where `V(n) = ψ(n)/n − 1`. As long as the current bound `α` is still at least `ε`,
the improvement lemma lowers it by the fixed amount `δ(ε)`. So after finitely many steps,
`|V(n)| < ε` for all large `n`. Since `ε` is arbitrary, `ψ(N)/N → 1`, and the equivalences of
`PNTEquivalence` turn this into `θ(N)/N → 1` and `π(N) log N / N → 1`.

# Unifying the Dirichlet and PNT blocks

This part of the library grew two independent towers on top of `Chebyshev`:

* the **Dirichlet block** (`ArithmeticFunctions` … `Dirichlet`, namespace
  `Foundations.NumberTheory`), which works with the generic field sum `gsum`, the logarithm

# Corollaries: Euler's divergence and a consequence of the prime number theorem

With the two blocks of this part unified (file `Unify`), we harvest two classical consequences.

**Euler (1737): `Σ 1/p` diverges.** Euler deduced it from his product formula; we deduce it from
Mertens' second theorem (`PNT.mertens_primes`), `Σ_{p ≤ N} log p / p = log N + O(1)`. Comparing the
values at `M` and `M²`, the primes in `(M, M²]` contribute about `log M` to `Σ log p / p`; each of
them has `log p ≤ 2 log M`, so they contribute at least about `1/2` to `Σ 1/p` — at least `1/4`
once `log M` is large (`primeRecip_block`). Squaring again and again (`M, M², M⁴, …`) adds `1/4`
each time, so `Σ_{p ≤ N} 1/p` is unbounded (`euler_sum_reciprocal_primes`). This replaces the
partial summation one would otherwise use.

**`π(2N) ∼ 2 π(N)`.** From the prime number theorem `π(N) log N / N → 1`, applied at `N` and at
`2N`, together with `log N / log 2N → 1`, the ratio `π(2N) / π(N)` tends to `2`
(`primeCount_two_mul_div_tendsto`): asymptotically there are as many primes in `(N, 2N]` as in
`[1, N]` — a quantitative refinement of Bertrand's postulate, and the reason the primes in
`(N, 2N]` become ever more numerous (`primeCount_two_mul_sub_unbounded`).

**Dirichlet in Euler's form.** Re-running the sieve argument of `DirichletConditional` with the
non-vanishing `L(1, χ) ≠ 0` now available, the sum `Σ_{n ≤ N, n ≡ a} Λ(n)/n` is unbounded; the
prime powers `pᵏ`, `k ≥ 2`, contribute at most `4`, so `Σ_{p ≤ N, p ≡ a (q)} log p / p` is
unbounded too (`dirichlet_euler`).

# Part XII: Number theory — the distribution of the primes

Euclid showed that the primes never run out. This part asks the next questions: *how* are they
distributed, and how far apart can they be? It builds on the arithmetic of Part II (primes,
Euclid's lemma, unique factorisation, factorials, the real logarithm) and on the quadratic
residues of Part IV.

1. `PrimesMod4` — infinitely many primes `≡ 3 (mod 4)` (Euclid's argument with `4·N! − 1`) and
   infinitely many primes `≡ 1 (mod 4)` (via `(2·N!)² + 1` and the first supplement to quadratic
   reciprocity). These are the simplest cases of **Dirichlet's theorem** (1837) on primes in
   arithmetic progressions, whose general proof needs analysis (L-functions) and is given in
   the files `Characters` … `Dirichlet` (theorem `dirichlet`).
2. `Binomial` — binomial coefficients via Pascal's rule; the central binomial coefficient
   `C(2n, n)` with `4ⁿ/(2n+1) ≤ C(2n, n) ≤ 4ⁿ`; the `p`-adic valuation and **Legendre's
   formula** `vₚ(n!) = Σ ⌊n/pᵏ⌋`; prime powers dividing `C(2n, n)` are at most `2n`, and primes
   in `(2n/3, n]` do not divide it.
3. `PrimorialBound` — Erdős's bound: the product of the primes up to `n` is at most `4ⁿ`.
4. `Bertrand` — **Bertrand's postulate** (conjectured 1845, proved by Chebyshev 1852): for every
   `n ≥ 1` there is a prime in `(n, 2n]`. We follow Erdős's elementary proof of 1932, which
   simplified Ramanujan's of 1919; small `n` are settled by a chain of twelve primes up to 1259,
   checked by the kernel.
5. `Chebyshev` — **Chebyshev's bounds**: `⌊m/2⌋ · log 2 ≤ π(m) · log m ≤ m · log 1024` for
   `m ≥ 6`, so `π(m)` is of order `m / log m`.

The **prime number theorem**, `π(x) ∼ x / log x`, is **proved** here
(`prime_number_theorem` in `PNTTheorem`, namespace `Foundations.NumberTheory.PNT`), by the

# Complete Boolean algebras

## Why truth values other than "true" and "false"?

In 1938 Kurt Gödel showed that the Continuum Hypothesis (CH: every infinite set of reals
is either countable or of the size of ℝ) cannot be *refuted* from the axioms of ZF set
theory with choice: inside any model of ZF he carved out the *constructible universe* `L`,
in which both choice and CH hold. In 1963 Paul Cohen proved the converse, that CH cannot be
*proved* either. His method, **forcing**, enlarges a model by adjoining a "generic" object
whose properties are decided only piecemeal, by finite pieces of information called
*conditions*.

Shortly afterwards Dana Scott and Robert Solovay, and independently Petr Vopěnka,
recast forcing as a semantics with many truth values. Instead of asking whether a sentence
is true in a model, one computes its **Boolean truth value** `⟦φ⟧`, an element of a complete
Boolean algebra `B`. The sentence "holds" in the Boolean-valued model when `⟦φ⟧ = ⊤`. If
`B` is the two-element algebra this is ordinary Tarskian semantics. For richer `B`, the
quantifiers become infinite meets and joins, which is why *completeness* (every family has a
supremum and an infimum) is required.

This file sets up complete Boolean algebras from scratch (there is no Mathlib here) and
proves the small lemma library the rest of the `Forcing` part needs: lattice laws,
complements, the Heyting implication `a ⇨ b = aᶜ ⊔ b` with its adjunction
`c ≤ a ⇨ b ↔ c ⊓ a ≤ b`, and **infinite distributivity** `a ⊓ ⨆ᵢ bᵢ = ⨆ᵢ (a ⊓ bᵢ)`, which is
what makes the existential quantifier behave.

The notation `⊓ ⊔ ᶜ ⊤ ⊥ ⇨ ⇔` is *scoped* to the namespace `Foundations.Forcing`, so it does
not clash with anything elsewhere in the library.

# The regular-open algebra of a forcing poset

Cohen's forcing works with a partial order of **conditions**: pieces of finite information
about a generic object, where `p ≤ q` means "`p` extends `q`" (it says at least as much).
Two conditions are **compatible** if some condition extends both.

To pass from forcing to Boolean-valued models one needs a *complete* Boolean algebra in which
the poset sits densely. The standard choice is the algebra of **regular open sets**. Give
the poset the topology whose open sets are the downward-closed sets (if `p` is in, so is
every extension of `p`). In this topology the interior of the closure of a set `S` is
`{p | ∀ q ≤ p, ∃ r ≤ q, r ∈ S}`, "below every extension of `p` there is a point of `S`",
and an open set is **regular** when it equals the interior of its closure. Here we work
with this combinatorial description directly, without the general topology part of the
library:

* a regular open set is a downward-closed `U` such that if every extension of `p` has a
  further extension in `U`, then `p ∈ U`;
* meets are intersections; joins are the regularisation of unions;
* the complement of `U` is `{p | no extension of p lies in U}`.

The main theorem `RO.instCBA` shows that these regular open sets form a complete Boolean
algebra `RO P`. Distributivity and the law of the excluded middle `U ⊔ Uᶜ = ⊤`
are exactly where regularity is used: the union of `U` and its pseudo-complement is not
all of `P`, but it is *dense*, and its regularisation is everything.

# Boolean-valued semantics for first-order logic

Tarski's semantics (`Logic/FOSemantics`) assigns to every formula, under an environment, a
truth value in `Prop`. Scott and Solovay's idea is to let truth values range over an
arbitrary complete Boolean algebra `B`:

* `⟦⊥⟧ = ⊥`, `⟦φ ∧ ψ⟧ = ⟦φ⟧ ⊓ ⟦ψ⟧`, `⟦φ ∨ ψ⟧ = ⟦φ⟧ ⊔ ⟦ψ⟧`, `⟦φ → ψ⟧ = ⟦φ⟧ ⇨ ⟦ψ⟧`;
* `⟦∀x φ⟧ = ⨅ₓ ⟦φ⟧[x]` and `⟦∃x φ⟧ = ⨆ₓ ⟦φ⟧[x]`, infinite meets and joins over the domain.

Equality is no longer two-valued either: a **Boolean-valued structure** (`BStructure`)
carries a `B`-valued equality `⟦x = y⟧`. It must be reflexive, symmetric and transitive in
the Boolean sense, and function and relation symbols must respect it (for instance
`⟦a = b⟧ ⊓ ⟦R a⟧ ≤ ⟦R b⟧`). In the Boolean-valued universe of set theory two distinct
names may denote "partly the same" set, so this generality is essential.

This file defines the truth value `val M e φ ∈ B` for the existing de Bruijn syntax and
proves the two technical lemmas that make the semantics behave:

* the **substitution lemma** `val_subst`, as in the Tarskian case;
* the **congruence lemma** `envEq_inf_val_le`: if two environments agree to degree
  `d = ⨅ₙ ⟦e n = e' n⟧`, then `d ⊓ ⟦φ⟧ₑ ≤ ⟦φ⟧ₑ'`. Every formula is extensional with
  respect to Boolean equality. This needs the *infinite* meet over all variables, which
  exists because `B` is complete.

Soundness of the proof calculus is proved in the next file.

Domains may live in any universe (`Type w`), because the Boolean-valued universe of sets
built later lives in `Type 1`. For this reason term evaluation and environments are
redefined here rather than borrowed from the `Prop`-valued development, whose domains live
in `Type`.

# Soundness of natural deduction for Boolean-valued models

The first-order natural deduction calculus `Γ ⊢₁ φ` of `Logic/FOSoundness` was shown sound
for Tarskian (two-valued) structures. Here we prove that it is sound for **every
Boolean-valued structure**, over every complete Boolean algebra `B`:

`Γ ⊢₁ φ  →  ⨅_{ψ ∈ Γ} ⟦ψ⟧ₑ ≤ ⟦φ⟧ₑ`  for every `B`-valued structure and environment `e`.

In particular a formula derivable from no premises has truth value `⊤`. This is the hinge
of the Boolean-valued approach to independence. To show that a theory `T` does not prove
`φ`, it suffices to find a complete Boolean algebra `B` and a `B`-valued model in which
every axiom of `T` has value `⊤` but `⟦φ⟧ ≠ ⊤`. Scott and Solovay showed that for
`T = ZFC` and `φ = CH` such a model exists (`V^B` for the Cohen algebra `B`). Here this is
carried out for `T = ZF` in `NotCH` (`ZF_not_proves_CH`), and for `T = ZFC` in
`AxiomOfChoice` and `Independence` (`CH_independent_ZFC`).

Each rule is checked against the algebra:

* `→`-introduction is residuation `c ⊓ a ≤ b ↔ c ≤ a ⇨ b`;
* reductio ad absurdum is the Boolean law `c ⊓ aᶜ ≤ ⊥ → c ≤ a`;
* `∨`-elimination is finite distributivity, `∃`-elimination is *infinite*
  distributivity `c ⊓ ⨆ₓ aₓ ≤ ⨆ₓ (c ⊓ aₓ)`;
* the quantifier rules use the substitution lemma, and Leibniz's law uses the
  congruence lemma of the previous file.

Finally, `Prop` is itself a complete Boolean algebra (classically). Every Tarskian structure
is a `Prop`-valued structure whose truth values are exactly Tarskian satisfaction
(`val_ofStructure_iff`). So the soundness theorem of `Logic/FOSoundness` is recovered as the
special case `B = Prop` (`entails_of_proves`).

# The Boolean-valued universe `V^B`

Aczel's pre-sets (`Sets/PSet`) model the cumulative hierarchy: a set is an indexed family
of earlier sets. Scott and Solovay's Boolean-valued universe `V^B` is the same idea with
*fuzzy* membership. A **`B`-valued pre-set** (`BSet B`, following the `bSet` of Han and van
Doorn's *flypitch* project) is an index type `α`, a family `A : α → BSet B` of earlier
names, and for each index a truth value `b i ∈ B`, the degree to which `A i` belongs.
In the forcing literature such objects are called **names**: a name does not yet denote a
definite set; it denotes "the set containing `A i` with probability `b i`".

Membership and equality are then defined by simultaneous recursion, as in `PSet.Equiv`:

* `⟦x = y⟧ = ⨅ᵢ (aᵢ ⇨ ⨆ⱼ (bⱼ ⊓ ⟦Aᵢ = Bⱼ⟧)) ⊓ ⨅ⱼ (bⱼ ⇨ ⨆ᵢ (aᵢ ⊓ ⟦Aᵢ = Bⱼ⟧))`
  ("every member of `x` is in `y`, and vice versa", to the appropriate degree);
* `⟦x ∈ y⟧ = ⨆ⱼ (bⱼ ⊓ ⟦x = Bⱼ⟧)`.

If `B` is the two-element algebra this is Aczel's construction. The main results of this file are
that Boolean equality is reflexive (`eq_self`), symmetric (`eq_symm`) and transitive
(`eq_trans`), and that membership respects it on both sides (`mem_congr_left`,
`mem_congr_right`). Transitivity is the delicate one: it is proved by induction on the
first name with the other two arbitrary, and uses infinite distributivity in both
directions. These are exactly the hypotheses needed to turn `V^B` into a Boolean-valued
structure for the language of set theory, which is done in `BSetModel`.

We require `B : Type`, so that `BSet B` lives in `Type 1`, like `PSet`.

# `V^B` as a Boolean-valued model of set theory

The previous file built names and their Boolean equality and membership. Here we package
them as a Boolean-valued structure `VB B` for the first-order **language of set theory**
`LSet` (one binary relation symbol `∈`, no function symbols), so that the general
Boolean-valued semantics of `BooleanSemantics` applies to arbitrary set-theoretic
formulas. We then verify that the following axioms of ZF have truth value `⊤` in `V^B`, for
**every** complete Boolean algebra `B`:

* **Extensionality** `∀x ∀y (∀z (z ∈ x ↔ z ∈ y) → x = y)`;
* **Empty set** `∃x ∀y ¬(y ∈ x)`;
* **Pairing** `∀x ∀y ∃z ∀w (w ∈ z ↔ w = x ∨ w = y)`;
* **Union** `∀x ∃u ∀w (w ∈ u ↔ ∃y (y ∈ x ∧ w ∈ y))`;
* the **Separation scheme** `∀x ∃s ∀z (z ∈ s ↔ z ∈ x ∧ φ(z))`, for every formula `φ`, with
  arbitrary parameters;
* the **∈-induction scheme** `∀x ((∀y ∈ x) φ(y) → φ(x)) → ∀x φ(x)`, for every formula `φ`
  (the form of Foundation used in ZF without choice).

Separation and ∈-induction hold for *all* formulas because of the congruence lemma of
`BooleanSemantics`: every formula is extensional for Boolean equality. The witness for
separation is the name `{(Aᵢ, bᵢ ⊓ ⟦φ(Aᵢ)⟧)}`, a direct Boolean analogue of
`{a ∈ x | φ(a)}`.

Combined with soundness, every first-order consequence of these axioms has value `⊤` in
`V^B` (`VB_val_eq_top_of_proves`). The remaining ZF axioms (power set, infinity and
collection) are verified in the next file, `BSetZF`. Choice is verified in `AxiomOfChoice`.

# Cohen forcing and the countable chain condition

To violate CH, Cohen adjoined `ℵ₂` new real numbers at once. A real is coded by a function
`ℕ → 2`, so `ℵ₂` reals form one function `I × ℕ → 2` with `|I| = ℵ₂`. A **Cohen condition** is a
*finite* piece of such a function: a finite partial function `p : J ⇀ Bool` (here
`J = I × ℕ`). `p` extends `q` if it agrees with `q` wherever `q` is defined. The **Cohen
algebra** is the regular-open algebra of this poset. Topologically it is the algebra of
regular open subsets of the Cantor space `2^J`, since conditions are exactly the basic
clopen sets. That identification is not formalised here: we *define* the Cohen algebra as
`RO (Cond J)`.

The decisive combinatorial property is the **countable chain condition (ccc)**: every
antichain is countable. In the forcing extension it guarantees that cardinals are not
collapsed, so the `ℵ₂` new reals really are `ℵ₂` many there. The usual proof goes through
the Δ-system lemma. We use a short induction on the size of the conditions instead:

> Let `A` be an antichain of conditions with at most `n + 1` points each, and fix `p₀ ∈ A`.
> Every other `q ∈ A` is incompatible with `p₀`, so `q` contradicts `p₀` at one of the
> finitely many points `j` of `p₀`'s domain. For a fixed `j`, erasing `j` from the
> conditions of `A` that contradict `p₀` at `j` is injective and gives an antichain of
> conditions with at most `n` points. By induction each of these finitely many families is
> countable, and so is `A`.

This works for an **arbitrary** index type `J`, of any size (`cond_ccc`). We then
transfer ccc to the regular-open algebra (`RO.ccc_of_poset`): every family of pairwise
disjoint non-zero elements of the Cohen algebra is countable (`cohen_ccc`).

Finally, using Zorn's lemma from `Sets/Choice`, we derive the form in which ccc is used in
practice: in a ccc algebra every supremum `⨆ᵢ bᵢ` is already the supremum of a countable
subfamily (`ccc_iSup_countable`).

# Cohen reals in the Boolean-valued universe

We now combine the two halves: the Boolean-valued universe `V^B` and the Cohen algebra
`B = Cohen I`. For each index `α ∈ I` there is a canonical name `ċ_α` for the `α`-th
**Cohen real**, the subset of `ω` whose characteristic function is the `α`-th row of the
generic function `I × ℕ → 2`:

`ċ_α = {(ň, ⟦the generic function takes value 1 at (α, n)⟧) | n ∈ ℕ}`,

where `ň` is the canonical name of the natural number `n` and the truth value is the
regular open set of conditions `p` with `p(α, n) = 1`.

The theorems of this file are the first genuinely *forcing-theoretic* facts proved here.
Each rests on a **density argument**: any condition can be extended to decide a fresh
coordinate either way.

* `creal_subset_omega`: `⟦ċ_α ⊆ ω̌⟧ = ⊤`, so each `ċ_α` is a set of natural numbers, i.e. a
  real.
* `creal_ne`: `⟦ċ_α = ċ_β⟧ = ⊥` for `α ≠ β`. The Cohen reals are pairwise distinct with
  Boolean value `⊤`. This is an external statement, one for each pair `α ≠ β`. The internal
  function `α ↦ ċ_α` is never built as a name; `NotCH` works with the external family.
* `creal_ne_ground`: `⟦ċ_α = ǎ⟧ = ⊥` for every ground-model set `a ⊆ ℕ`. The Cohen reals
  are **new**: none of them was already in the ground model.

All three are non-vacuous because the Cohen algebra is non-degenerate, `⊤ ≠ ⊥`
(`cohen_top_ne_bot`): a value `⊥` is genuinely different from `⊤`.

# Set-theoretic notions as formulas, and their Boolean truth values

To state the Continuum Hypothesis as a sentence of the first-order language `LSet` (whose
only non-logical symbol is `∈`), we build up the usual definitions as formula
combinators: `x ⊆ y`, ordered pairs, "`f` is a function from `X` to `Y`", "`f` is
injective on `X`", "`w` is `ω`" and "`p` is the power set of `w`". Each combinator takes
*terms* as arguments and lifts them past its own quantifiers with `up`, so combinators nest
freely.

For each combinator we compute its truth value in `V^B` as an explicit Boolean expression in
names (`val_subsetF`, `val_pmF`, `val_isFuncF`, …). Ordered pairs are Kuratowski pairs: the
formula "`z = (a, b)`" has value exactly `⟦z = {{a, a}, {a, b}}⟧` (`val_opairF`), and
"`(a, b) ∈ f`" has value `⟦(a, b) ∈ f⟧` for the pair name (`val_pmF`).

Functions are coded as usual by sets of pairs. `isFuncF f X Y` says: every `a ∈ X` has some
`b ∈ Y` with `(a, b) ∈ f`, and for `a ∈ X` such a `b` is unique. Elements of `f` outside `X × Y`
are not forbidden. For statements "there is a function/injection from `X` to `Y`" this is
equivalent to the textbook definition (restrict `f`), an informal remark that is not
formalised.

Finally `CH` is the sentence

> for all `w`, `p`: if `w = ω` and `p = 𝒫(w)`, then every `x ⊆ p` admits an injection into
> `w` or receives an injection from `p`,

that is, every subset of `𝒫(ω)` is countable or has the cardinality of `𝒫(ω)`. Here "`w = ω`"
is expressed as "`w` is inductive and contained in every inductive set".

# The countable chain condition preserves cardinals

Why does adding `ℵ₂` Cohen reals not simply collapse `ℵ₂` to something smaller, making the
new reals too few after all? Because the Cohen algebra is **ccc**. Here is the Boolean form of
the classical argument. Suppose that in `V^B` some `f` is, to degree `d`, an injective
function from a name `X = {xₜ | t ∈ T}` (pairwise Boolean-distinct members) into a name
`Y = {yᵤ | u ∈ U}`.

* For each `t`, `d ≤ ⨆ᵤ ⟦(xₜ, yᵤ) ∈ f⟧`, since `f` is total on `X`.
* For each fixed `u`, the values `d ⊓ ⟦(xₜ, yᵤ) ∈ f⟧` for different `t` are pairwise disjoint,
  since `f` is injective and the `xₜ` are distinct. By ccc only countably many of them are
  non-zero.
* If `d ≠ ⊥`, choosing for every `t` some `u` with non-zero value gives an injection of `T`
  into `U × ℕ`.

So if `T` does **not** inject into `U × ℕ` (in the ground model), then `d = ⊥`: in `V^B` there is
no injection from `X` into `Y` (`isFunc_inf_isInj_eq_bot`). Cardinals that differ in the ground
model by more than a factor `ℵ₀` stay apart in the extension.

The second half of the file sets up the ground-model cardinals used later: `W₁`, the members
of the Hartogs ordinal `ℵ(ℕ) = ω₁`, and `W₂`, the members of `ℵ(W₁) = ω₂`. It proves the two
non-injectivity facts that are needed: `W₁ ↛ ℕ × ℕ` and `W₂ ↛ W₁ × ℕ`, the latter via
`κ · κ = κ` from `Sets/CardinalArith`.

# The Lévy collapse of the continuum onto `ω₁`: the forcing poset

`NotCH` showed that ZF does not prove CH. The other half of the independence of CH is that
ZF does not refute it either. **Gödel (1938)** proved this by building, inside any model of
ZF, the constructible universe `L`, in which CH holds. Formalising `L` would need the whole
theory of definability inside set theory. Here we take the forcing route instead. Forcing
can make CH *true* as easily as false: **collapse** the continuum onto `ω₁`.

This idea goes back to **Lévy (1963)**, whose collapsing posets make a given cardinal
countable or of size `ℵ₁`. The poset used here is the version that collapses `2^ℵ₀` onto
`ℵ₁`:

> a condition is a **countable** partial function `p : ω₁ ⇀ 𝒫(ℕ)`, and `p ≤ q` when `p`
> extends `q`.

The generic object is a function from `ω₁` onto the ground-model reals. Its decisive property
is **σ-closure**: every descending sequence `p₀ ≥ p₁ ≥ p₂ ≥ …` has a lower bound, namely the
union (`sigma_closed`). This is the exact opposite of the countable chain condition of Cohen
forcing. ccc forcing preserves cardinals but adds many reals. σ-closed forcing adds **no new
countable sequences**, so no new reals and no new countable sets of ordinals, while it may
collapse cardinals above `ℵ₁`.

This file sets up:

* `Omega1Like I`: the properties of `ω₁` that are used (a well-order, all of whose initial
  segments are countable, which is itself uncountable), with the instance for the ground
  `ω₁ = W₁` of `CardinalPreservation` (`instOmega1LikeW₁`), and the regularity fact that
  countable subsets are bounded (`Omega1Like.exists_bound`);
* the conditions `CCond I` and their extension order, the existence of fresh points
  (`CCond.exists_fresh`), one-point extensions, and **σ-closure** (`CCond.sigma_closed`);
* the collapse algebra `Col I = RO (CCond I)`, its non-degeneracy (`col_top_ne_bot`) and
  small helpers for computing in regular-open algebras;
* the atoms `⟦g(ξ) = a⟧` of the generic function, which are pairwise disjoint in `a`
  (`catom_disj`) and dense in `ξ` (`top_le_iSup_catom`): every ground real is a value of `g`;
* the **deciding lemma** `decide_countable`, the Boolean-valued form of "σ-closed forcing adds
  no new countable sequences": below any condition, countably many questions, each of which
  has an answer with value `⊤`, are all answered by a single condition.

# Boolean-valued enumeration of subsets of `ω₁`

The last step of the proof of CH in the collapse model is a fact of ZF: an uncountable subset
`A` of `ω₁` has cardinality `ℵ₁`, because its increasing enumeration `f : ω₁ → A`,

`f(α) = the least element of A above all f(β), β < α`,

is an injection. In the Boolean-valued universe `A` is given by truth values
`b ξ = ⟦ξ ∈ A⟧`, one for each ground ordinal `ξ < ω₁`, and `A` need not be in the ground
model. Rather than re-proving ordinal theory inside `V^B`, we define the enumeration
*externally*, by well-founded recursion on the ground ordinal `α`, as a family of truth
values `enumV b α ζ = ⟦f(α) = ζ⟧`:

`⟦f(α) = ζ⟧ = b ζ ⊓ ⨅_{η < ζ} (b η ⇨ ⨆_{β < α} ⟦f(β) = η⟧) ⊓ ⨅_{β < α} ⨆_{η < ζ} ⟦f(β) = η⟧`,

"`ζ ∈ A`, every element of `A` below `ζ` has already been enumerated, and every earlier value
lies below `ζ`". Everything in this file holds in every complete Boolean algebra, over every
`ω₁`-like order (in fact only the well-order is used):

* the **least-element principle** for Boolean families, `⨆ d ≤ ⨆_ξ (d ξ ⊓ ⨅_{η<ξ} (d η)ᶜ)`
  (`iSup_le_iSup_least`), the Boolean form of the well-ordering of the ground `ω₁`;
* `f` is **single-valued** (`enumV_disj`) and **injective** (`enumV_inj`);
* the **step**: if some element of `A` lies above all earlier values, then `f(α)` is defined
  (`enumV_step`).

Whether some element of `A` lies above all earlier values is the one place where σ-closure is
needed. That is done in `CollapseCH`.

# σ-closed forcing adds no new reals

The heart of the collapse argument is the observation, going back to the earliest days of
forcing, that a **σ-closed** poset adds no new subsets of `ω`. A name for a set of natural
numbers asks countably many questions "is `n` in?", and by σ-closure a single condition below
any given one answers all of them. So the name is, below that condition, equal to the check
name of a ground-model real. In Boolean-valued form:

> **No new reals** (`mem_powersetB_le`). In `V^{Col I}`, every member of `𝒫(ω̌)` is a mixture
> of ground reals: `⟦z ∈ 𝒫(ω̌)⟧ ≤ ⨆_{a ⊆ ℕ} ⟦z = ǎ⟧`.

Here `𝒫(ω̌)` is the standard power-set name `powersetB` of `NotCH`, whose members are the
Boolean subsets `ω̌↾f` for `f : ℕ → B`. For each such `f` the deciding lemma
`decide_countable` gives, below any condition, a condition `r` deciding every value `f n`;
then `r` forces `ω̌↾f = ǎ` with `a = {n | r decides n ∈}` (`top_le_iSup_eq_ground`).

The second half of the file sets up the generic function `g : I → 𝒫(ℕ)` as a tool: the truth
value `fo ξ a = ⟦g(ξ) = a ∧ ∀η < ξ, g(η) ≠ a⟧` that `ξ` is the **first occurrence** of the
ground real `a` in the generic sequence. Every real has exactly one first occurrence

`I = ω₁`; this is how the generic surjection `ω₁ → 𝒫(ω)` is used in `CollapseCH`, without

# Sanity checks: the CH encoding is not trivially false

`NotCH` proves `⟦CH⟧ = ⊥` in `V^{Cohen(ω₂)}` and concludes `ZF ⊬ CH`. A proof of that shape
is only as good as the sentence `CH`. If the encoding were defective, `⟦CH⟧ = ⊥` could hold
for reasons that have nothing to do with the continuum. For example:

* if the formula for "`f` is an injective function from `X` to `Y`" could never have value
  `⊤`, every instance of "`X` injects into `Y`" would be `⊥`, and so would `CH`;
* if the Kuratowski pair coding lost information, "injective" might mean something else;
* if "`w = ω`" or "`p = 𝒫(w)`" were satisfied by the wrong names (or by none), the
  quantifiers `∀w ∀p` in `CH` would range over the wrong objects.

This file rules these failure modes out by direct computation, in every `V^B` and in the
very model `V^{Cohen(ω₂)}` used by `NotCH`. Nothing here is needed for the main theorem. The
file is an audit: it shows that the formula `CH` says what it is meant to say, on enough test
cases that a vacuous encoding would have been caught.

1. **Kuratowski pairs are injective in the Boolean sense** (`opair_inj`):
   `⟦(a, b) = (c, d)⟧ ≤ ⟦a = c⟧ ⊓ ⟦b = d⟧`.
2. **Injections exist when they should.** The identity relation on `X` is an injective
   function `X → Y` with value `⊤` whenever `X ⊆ Y` (`idName_injfunc`). Any `f` is an injective
   function from the empty name with value `⊤` (`empty_injfunc`). The graph of a family of
   pairwise Boolean-distinct names is injective (`graph_injfunc`).
3. **The CH matrix is satisfiable in `V^{Cohen(ω₂)}`.** `ω̌` injects into the witness `x` of
   `NotCH` (`omega_inj_xName`, so `V^B` sees that `x` is infinite). The matrix of `CH` has

4. **The definitions of `ω` and `𝒫(ω)` pin down unique objects.** Anything satisfying "`w = ω`"

   Boolean-equal (`isPow_unique`). So the outer quantifiers of `CH` effectively range over the

# Disjoint refinements, the mixing lemma and the maximum principle

To verify the axiom of choice in `V^B` (next file, `AxiomOfChoice`) we need two classical
tools of Boolean-valued model theory (Bell, *Set Theory: Boolean-Valued Models and
Independence Proofs*, ch. 1).

* **Disjoint refinement.** In a complete Boolean algebra, a family `(f i)` indexed by a
  well-ordered type can be cut down to `g i = f i ⊓ ¬⨆_{k<i} f k`. The `g i` are pairwise
  disjoint and have the same supremum. We prove a relative version, with a "similarity"
  `r i k` (later: Boolean equality of names): `g i = f i ⊓ ¬⨆_{k<i} (f k ⊓ r i k)`. Then
  `g i ⊓ g k ⊓ r i k = ⊥` for `i ≠ k` (`refine_disjoint`), and every `f i` is covered by
  `⨆ₖ (g k ⊓ r i k)` (`refine_cover`, by well-founded induction). The well-ordering comes
  from Zermelo's theorem in the metatheory (`Sets/Choice`, proved from Zorn's lemma).
* **The mixing lemma.** Given names `y t` and pairwise disjoint weights `w t`, the name
  `mix w y`, which lists each member of `y t` with its degree cut down by `w t`, is equal to
  `y t` to degree at least `w t` (`le_eq_mix`). This needs no choice at all.

Together they give the **maximum principle** (Bell's fullness of `V^B`): every existential
truth value is attained by a single name. For any formula `φ` there is a name `z` with
`⨆_y ⟦φ(y)⟧ ≤ ⟦φ(z)⟧` (`VB_maximum_principle`). We only need the special case "every nonempty
name has a member" (`BSet.exists_mem_witness`): there is `z` with `⨆_w ⟦w ∈ Y⟧ ≤ ⟦z ∈ Y⟧`.

# The axiom of choice in `V^B`, and ZFC ⊬ CH

`NotCH` showed `ZF ⊬ CH`. To upgrade this to Cohen's theorem in its usual form, `ZFC ⊬ CH`, we
verify that the axiom of choice has truth value `⊤` in `V^B` for **every** complete Boolean
algebra `B`. We use the **choice-set form** of AC (Zermelo 1908; Jech, *Set Theory*, ch. 5):

> for every set `x` whose members are nonempty and pairwise disjoint, there is a set `c` that
> meets every member of `x` in exactly one element.

Over the other axioms of ZF this is equivalent to the usual forms of AC (choice functions,
well-ordering, Zorn). That equivalence is textbook set theory and is not formalised here.

**The proof.** Let `x = {(Xᵢ, aᵢ)}` and assume the hypothesis of AC to degree `H`. Two choices
must be made coherently.

1. *Which listed members represent a member of `x`.* Different indices `i ≠ k` may list
   Boolean-equal members `Xᵢ`, `Xₖ`. A choice made separately for each would then violate
   uniqueness. So we well-order the index type in the metatheory and pass to the
   disjoint refinement `sᵢ = aᵢ ⊓ ¬⨆_{k<i} (aₖ ⊓ ⟦Xᵢ = Xₖ⟧)` of `Mixing`. Then

The two halves of the independence of the Continuum Hypothesis come from two different

# Part: Forcing and Boolean-valued models: CH is independent of ZFC

## The problem

Cantor's **Continuum Hypothesis** (1878) says that every infinite set of real numbers is
either countable or in bijection with ℝ; equivalently `2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₁`. Hilbert put it first on his
list of problems in 1900. The answer came in two halves:

* **Gödel (1938)**: CH cannot be *refuted* in ZF set theory with choice (ZFC). Inside any
  model of ZF Gödel built the **constructible universe** `L` of sets that are definable
  from earlier ones, stage by stage along the ordinals. In `L` both the axiom of choice and
  CH hold. So if ZF is consistent, so is ZFC + CH.
* **Cohen (1963)**: CH cannot be *proved* in ZFC either. His method, **forcing**, extends a
  countable model `M` by a "generic" object `G` that `M` cannot describe. The truth of a
  statement in `M[G]` is decided by finite pieces of information about `G` (the
  conditions). Adding `ℵ₂` generic reals makes `2^ℵ₀ ≥ ℵ₂`.

**Scott, Solovay and Vopěnka** (1965–67) recast forcing as **Boolean-valued model theory**:
instead of building `M[G]`, assign to each sentence `φ` a truth value `⟦φ⟧` in a complete
Boolean algebra `B`. Every axiom of ZF(C) gets value `⊤`, and for the Cohen algebra so does
`¬CH`. Soundness of first-order logic for such models then shows that CH is not provable.
This is the route taken here. It is also the route of the Lean 3 *flypitch* project (Han
and van Doorn, 2019), which completed the independence proof (both halves, for ZFC) with
Mathlib. Here both halves are proved, for ZF and then for ZFC: Cohen's half with the Cohen algebra,
and Gödel's half with a collapse algebra instead of `L` (item 10), with choice verified in every
`V^B` (item 13); the conclusion is `CH_independent_ZFC` (item 14).

## What independence means

That CH is independent of ZFC is a *mathematical* theorem about formal provability. It
holds whatever one believes about sets. Its philosophical weight is contested. For a
formalist the question "is CH true?" has no further content once independence is known.
Gödel himself held the realist view: CH has a definite truth value, and he expected it to
be false. Independence then shows that the ZFC axioms are an incomplete description of the
universe of sets, and new axioms (large cardinals, forcing axioms) must be sought. Others,
such as Hamkins with his "multiverse", read forcing as revealing many equally legitimate
set-theoretic universes, in some of which CH holds and in others not. Boolean-valued models
make the technical core vivid: a statement may be neither true nor false but true *to a
degree*, and unprovability is the existence of a coherent assignment of degrees in which the
axioms are fully true and the statement is not.

# Relativised satisfaction: formulas of set theory read inside a class

## Gödel's idea

In 1938 Kurt Gödel showed that the axiom of choice and the generalised continuum
hypothesis cannot be refuted from the axioms of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory. His method was
to find, inside any universe of sets, a smaller universe `L` of **constructible** sets in
which these statements are true. The sets of `L` are built in stages along the ordinals, and
at each stage one adds exactly those subsets of the previous stage that can be **defined**
over it by a first-order formula of set theory. Everything in this part rests on that one
notion: a formula `φ` of the language `LSet` (one binary relation symbol `∈`) can be read
inside a structure `(X, ∈)`, with its quantifiers ranging only over `X`.

## What this file does

For a predicate `P : ZFSet → Prop` (a "class") we define `RSat P e φ`: the formula `φ` holds
when its quantifiers range over the sets satisfying `P`, membership is real membership and the
free variables take the values `e n`. This is the familiar **relativisation** `φ^P` of set
theory. Two special cases connect it with the library's existing semantics:

* for a set `X`, the Tarskian structure `setStr X` with domain `Small X` (a small type of the
  members of `X`, from the forcing part) satisfies `φ` exactly when `RSat (· ∈ X)` does
  (`sat_setStr_iff`);
* for a class `P`, the two-valued Boolean structure `classStr P` with domain the subtype
  `{z // P z}` (which lives in `Type 1`) gives `φ` the truth value `⊤` exactly when
  `RSat P` holds (`val_classStr_iff`). This is the form in which soundness
  (`not_proves_of_val`) applies.

We prove the substitution lemma for `RSat` and a **finite support** lemma: the truth of `φ`
depends only on the values of the variables below a syntactic bound `bnd φ`. The latter lets
us replace an environment of infinitely many parameters by one with finitely many, which is
needed in the reflection argument later.

## The contrast with forcing

Part XIII proved both halves of the independence of CH by *enlarging* the universe: a
Boolean-valued model `V^B` adds new, generic sets. Gödel's method goes the other way: it
*shrinks* the universe to the sets that are explicitly definable from earlier ones. Here
the truth values are two-valued again (`B = Prop`), and the domain is a subclass of the
ordinary universe `ZFSet`.

# The definable power set `Def(X)`

## Definability

The power set `𝒫(X)` contains *every* subset of `X`, including the ones no description can
pick out. Gödel's construction replaces it by the much thinner **definable power set**

  `Def(X) = { {y ∈ X | (X, ∈) ⊨ φ[y, a₁, …, aₙ]} | φ a formula of LSet, a₁, …, aₙ ∈ X }`,

the subsets of `X` that are first-order definable over the structure `(X, ∈)` from finitely
many parameters taken from `X` itself. The quantifiers of `φ` range only over `X`: a set is
admitted at the next stage only if it can be described using what is already there. This is
the "predicative" step that, iterated along the ordinals, builds the constructible universe
`L` in the next file.

## The formal definition

Satisfaction is the library's Tarskian `Formula.Sat` in the structure `setStr X`, whose domain
is the small type `Small X` of members of `X`. An environment `e : ℕ → Small X` supplies the
parameters; only the finitely many variables occurring in `φ` matter. Because a structure with
empty domain has no environments, the empty set is added by hand: `Def(X)` is `{∅}` together with
all sets `defSet X φ e`. For non-empty `X` this adds nothing new, since `∅` is defined by `⊥`.
Both `Formula LSet` and `ℕ → Small X` live in `Type`, so the family of definable subsets is
indexed by a small type and `Def(X)` is a genuine `ZFSet`.

The working characterisation `mem_Def` re-expresses everything through the relativised
satisfaction `RSat (· ∈ X)` of the previous file, with parameters as plain sets.

## Closure properties

`Def(X) ⊆ 𝒫(X)`, `∅ ∈ Def(X)`, `X ∈ Def(X)`, every finite subset of `X` is in `Def(X)`, and
`Def(X)` is a Boolean algebra of subsets of `X` (closed under complement, binary union and binary
intersection). If `X` is transitive then `X ⊆ Def(X)`: each member `a` of `X` is the subset
`{y ∈ X | y ∈ a}`, defined with the parameter `a`.

# The constructible hierarchy `L_α` and the class `L`

## Gödel's hierarchy

Gödel (1938) defined the constructible sets in stages:

  `L₀ = ∅`,  `L_{α+1} = Def(L_α)`,  `L_λ = ⋃_{β<λ} L_β` for limit `λ`,

and `L = ⋃_α L_α`. Compare the cumulative hierarchy `V_{α+1} = 𝒫(V_α)`: the only difference is
that the full power set is replaced by the definable one. That single change makes `L` a very
"thin" and very well-understood universe. Every constructible set has a description, a formula
together with finitely many earlier parameters, and this is what later yields a definable
well-ordering of `L` and the generalised continuum hypothesis in `L`. (Those consequences are
**not** formalised here; see the aggregator `Constructible` for the status.)

## How the recursion is set up

Ordinals in this library are von Neumann ordinals inside `ZFSet`, and there is no packaged
transfinite recursion for set-valued functions. We use the well-foundedness of `∈` on `ZFSet`
(from `∈`-induction) and Lean's `WellFounded.fix` to define, for *every* set `x`,

  `Lev x = ⋃_{y ∈ x} Def(Lev y)`.

This single uniform clause gives Gödel's three clauses on ordinals (`Lev_zero`, `Lev_succ`,
`Lev_limit`, gathered in `L_recursion`). It also makes monotonicity immediate: `x ⊆ y` gives
`Lev x ⊆ Lev y` (`Lev_mono`). For transitive `x` the stage `Lev x` is transitive
(`Lev_transitive`).

## The class `L`

`InL z` means `z ∈ L_α` for some ordinal `α`. The class is transitive (`InL.mem`). Any set of
constructible sets lies inside a single stage `L_α` (`exists_stage`); this uses replacement in
the ambient `ZFSet` universe. Every ordinal is constructible, and the ordinals of `L_α` are
exactly the members of `α` (`ordinals_Lev`).

# The reflection principle for `L` and the separation scheme in `L`

## Why reflection is needed

To show that `L` satisfies separation, take a constructible set `a`, constructible parameters
and a formula `φ`. The set `S = {z ∈ a | φ^L(z)}` must again be constructible. Each new
constructible set is definable over some *set* `L_α`, but `φ^L` quantifies over the whole
*class* `L`. The bridge is the **reflection principle** (Lévy–Montague, here for the
`L`-hierarchy): for every formula `φ` and every ordinal `β` there is an ordinal `α ⊇ β` such that
`φ` is **absolute** between `L_α` and `L`, i.e. for parameters in `L_α`,
`φ^L ↔ φ^{L_α}`. Then `S = {z ∈ a | φ^{L_α}(z)} ∈ Def(L_α) ⊆ L_{α+1}`.

## The proof

* **Tarski–Vaught step** (`absolute_of_closed`). Call `α` *closed* for a formula `χ` if
  whenever `∃y ∈ L χ(y, e)` with parameters `e` in `L_α`, there is already such a witness in
  `L_α`, and likewise for `¬χ`. If `α` is closed for the bodies of all quantifiers of `φ`, then `φ`
  is absolute for `L_α`. The proof is by induction on `φ`: connectives are immediate and each
  quantifier is handled by the closure condition.
* **Closing off** (`exists_closed`). Given finitely many formulas and an ordinal `β`, iterate
  `γ ↦ γ ∪ sup{chosen witness stages for all parameter lists from L_γ}` along `ℕ` and take the
  supremum `α`. Parameters from `L_α` occur already at a finite stage. Only the finitely many
  variables of a formula matter (`RSat_congr`), so a parameter list can be truncated to lie in a
  single `L_{γₙ}`. The suprema exist because the ambient universe `ZFSet` has replacement for
  arbitrary operations, and parameter lists `ℕ → Small (L_γ)` form a small type.

The result `separation_L` is the separation scheme for `L`, the step that needs the most
machinery among the ZF axioms. Collection and power set in `L` (next file) need only the
bounding lemma `exists_stage`, since the ambient universe already satisfies them.

# `L` is a model of ZF

## The theorem

Gödel's first main theorem about `L` (1938): **the constructible universe is a model of ZF.**
Here `L` is packaged as the two-valued structure `LModel = (L, ∈)` on the subtype
`{z : ZFSet // InL z}`. Every axiom of the theory `ZF` of Part XIII then has truth value `⊤`
(`L_models_ZF`). That theory consists of extensionality, empty set, pairing, union, power set,
infinity, and the separation, collection and `∈`-induction schemes, each with all its universal
closures.

## The proofs, axiom by axiom

* **Extensionality** and **`∈`-induction** hold because `L` is a transitive class
  (`InL.mem`): for constructible sets, "same constructible members" means "same members",
  and `∈`-induction in `ZFSet` restricts to `L`.
* **Empty set, pairing, union**: the required sets are separated out of a stage `L_α`
  that contains them, using `separation_L`.
* **Infinity**: the stage `L_ω` itself is a constructible set containing `∅` and closed under
  `x ↦ x ∪ {x}`.
* **Power set**: the constructible subsets of `x` all lie in one stage `L_β` (bounding), and
  `{z ∈ L_β | z ⊆ x}` is constructible by separation. It is the power set of `x` *in the sense
  of `L`*: it contains only the constructible subsets, which is the whole point.
* **Collection**: choose for each `x ∈ u` a constructible witness, bound all of them in one
  stage `L_β`, and take `v = L_β`.
* **Separation**: the reflection principle (`separation_L`, previous file).

The sets that `L` thinks are power sets are generally smaller than the real ones. This is
possible because "`p` is the power set of `x`" is *not* absolute. In contrast, the formulas used
for the empty set, pairs, unions and successors are absolute for transitive classes, so `L`
computes these operations correctly.

## Consequences

By soundness of the proof calculus for `Prop`-valued structures (`val_eq_top_of_theory`),
every theorem of ZF is true in `L` (`L_val_eq_top_of_ZF`). In particular ZF does not prove `⊥`
(`ZF_consistent_via_L`). That consequence was already available from the forcing models; here it
comes from an inner model, Gödel's route.

# Absoluteness of bounded formulas

## Why absoluteness matters

A statement about sets is **absolute** for a class `M` if it means the same thing whether its
quantifiers range over `M` or over the whole universe. Absoluteness is the central tool of
Gödel's theory of `L`. To prove that `V = L` holds *inside* `L`, one shows that the whole
construction `α ↦ L_α` is absolute for `L`, so that `L` computes its own hierarchy correctly. To
prove that choice and GCH hold in `L`, one uses that the definable well-ordering of `L` and the
condensation argument are absolute. Forcing has nothing comparable: a generic extension `M[G]`
contains sets that `M` cannot even name. Inner models like `L` agree with the universe on every
absolute statement.

## What is proved here

The basic absoluteness theorem: a **bounded** (`Δ₀`) formula, in which every quantifier is of
the form `∀y ∈ x` or `∃y ∈ x`, is absolute for every transitive class (`delta0_absolute`). The
proof is a direct induction: a bounded quantifier over `x ∈ M` only ever looks at members of
`x`, and these lie in `M` by transitivity.

Applied to `L`: being transitive and being an ordinal are bounded properties, so the ordinals of
`L` in the sense of `L` are the true ordinals (`L_ordinal_iff`). Together with `ordinals_Lev`
(every ordinal is constructible), `L` contains all ordinals and recognises them correctly.

The much harder absoluteness of the formula "`x ∈ L_α`" itself, which needs a set-theoretic
formalisation of the satisfaction relation inside `LSet`, is **not** done; see the aggregator
`Constructible`.

# Part: The constructible universe `L`

## Gödel 1938

Part XIII proved that the Continuum Hypothesis is independent of ZFC, with *both* halves done by
forcing over Boolean-valued models. Historically the first half came a quarter of a century
before forcing. In 1938 Kurt Gödel showed that CH, and with it the axiom of choice and the
generalised continuum hypothesis, cannot be refuted from ZF. He did it by finding inside the
universe of sets a smaller universe, the **constructible universe** `L`, in which they all hold.

## The definability idea

`L` is built in stages along the ordinals, like the cumulative hierarchy `V_α`, but the power-set
step `V_{α+1} = 𝒫(V_α)` is replaced by the **definable power set**:

  `L₀ = ∅`,  `L_{α+1} = Def(L_α)`,  `L_λ = ⋃_{β<λ} L_β`,  `L = ⋃_α L_α`,

where `Def(X)` consists of the subsets of `X` that are first-order definable over `(X, ∈)` with
parameters from `X`. A set enters `L` only if it can be *described*, by a formula of set theory,
in terms of sets that are already there. Russell and Poincaré's demand that sets be defined
"predicatively" is made precise and then pushed through the whole transfinite.

## Why `L` matters

* **`L` is a model of ZF** (proved here: `L_models_ZF`). So whatever ZF proves is true in `L`, and
  `L` is a second universe of sets sitting inside the first one.
* **`V = L` holds in `L`.** The construction of `L` is *absolute*: computed inside `L`, it gives
  `L` again. So ZF + `V = L` is consistent if ZF is. From `V = L` Gödel derived a definable
  well-ordering of the universe (hence AC) and, through the *condensation lemma*, GCH. This route
  gives Con(ZF) → Con(ZFC + GCH).
* `V = L` settles many questions that ZFC leaves open (Suslin's problem, the Whitehead problem,
  projective-set regularity) and is the prototype of all **inner models** in modern set theory.

## Contrast with forcing

Forcing *adds* sets: the generic extension `M[G]` contains objects `M` cannot describe, and truth
in it is decided by conditions. Gödel's `L` *removes* sets: it keeps only the describable ones.
Forcing shows that statements are unprovable by making them false; `L` shows that statements are
irrefutable by making them true. Absoluteness is the tool on the `L` side, genericity on the
forcing side. In this library the forcing part proved both halves of the independence of CH
(Gödel's half with a σ-closed collapse instead of `L`). This part supplies the inner model itself,
as far as described below.

# The `p`-adic valuation and the `p`-adic absolute value on ℚ

The integers carry, besides their familiar size, one notion of size for every prime `p`: an
integer is *`p`-adically small* when it is divisible by a high power of `p`. Kurt Hensel, in
1897, took this seriously and treated the expansion of an integer in powers of `p` as an analogue
of the Laurent expansion of a function at a point: each prime is a "point", and divisibility by
`p` is vanishing at that point. The resulting `p`-adic numbers are the subject of this part.

This first file turns the `p`-adic valuation `vₚ` on natural numbers — introduced in
`Foundations.NumberTheory.Binomial` for Legendre's formula — into a valuation on the rationals:
for `x = n/d ≠ 0`,

  `vₚ(x) = vₚ(|n|) − vₚ(d)`,

which is well defined on classes of fractions because `vₚ` is additive (Euclid's lemma). Its two
key properties are

* `vₚ(x y) = vₚ(x) + vₚ(y)`, and
* `vₚ(x + y) ≥ min(vₚ(x), vₚ(y))`.

The **`p`-adic absolute value** is `|x|ₚ = p^(−vₚ(x))` (and `|0|ₚ = 0`), a rational number. The
two properties above translate into multiplicativity `|x y|ₚ = |x|ₚ |y|ₚ` and the
**ultrametric inequality** `|x + y|ₚ ≤ max(|x|ₚ, |y|ₚ)`, much stronger than the triangle
inequality: in the `p`-adic world, adding small numbers never makes something big.

Everything here is ℚ-valued; the real-valued theory (needed for Ostrowski's theorem, where other
absolute values with irrational values appear) is in `Ostrowski`.

# The product formula

Every nonzero rational number `x` has one "size" for each place of ℚ: the ordinary absolute value
`|x|_∞` (the *infinite place*) and the `p`-adic absolute values `|x|ₚ`, one for each prime `p`
(the *finite places*). These sizes are not independent. Writing `x = ± ∏ p^(vₚ(x))` by the
fundamental theorem of arithmetic, `|x|_∞ = ∏ p^(vₚ(x))` while `|x|ₚ = p^(−vₚ(x))`, so

  `∏ₚ |x|ₚ · |x|_∞ = 1`.

Only finitely many factors differ from `1`, so the product is really finite. This
**product formula** is the simplest instance of the *local–global* philosophy: information at all
places together is constrained by a global identity. It is the arithmetic analogue of the fact
that a nonzero rational function on the Riemann sphere has as many zeros as poles, counted with
multiplicity — Hensel's analogy between primes and points again.

Concretely we prove: for every `x ≠ 0` there is `N` such that `|x|ₚ = 1` for all `p ≥ N`, and
the product of `|x|ₚ` over the primes `p < M` times `|x|_∞` equals `1` for every `M ≥ N`.

# Absolute values on ℚ

An **absolute value** on ℚ is a function `φ : ℚ → ℝ` that is non-negative, vanishes only at `0`,
is multiplicative and satisfies the triangle inequality. Two examples are already at hand: the
ordinary absolute value `|·|_∞` and, for each prime `p`, the `p`-adic absolute value `|·|ₚ` of
`Valuation`, now viewed as real-valued. Raising an absolute value to a power `s` with `0 < s ≤ 1`
gives another one, so absolute values are naturally considered up to **equivalence**:
`ψ ~ φ` when `ψ = φ^s` for some `s > 0`. To avoid real exponents we phrase this with the natural
logarithm of `Foundations.Numbers.Log`:

  `ψ ~ φ  :⇔  ∃ s > 0, ∀ x ≠ 0, log ψ(x) = s · log φ(x)`,

which is exactly `ψ(x) = exp(s · log φ(x)) = φ(x)^s`.

This file sets up the definitions, the two families of examples, the facts about logarithms we
need, and proves the easy half of Ostrowski's theorem: the absolute values `|·|_∞`, `|·|₂`,
`|·|₃`, `|·|₅`, … are pairwise inequivalent. The hard half — there are no others — is in
`Ostrowski`.

# Ostrowski's theorem, I: the digit bound

Alexander Ostrowski proved in 1916 that the absolute values on ℚ are, up to equivalence, exactly
`|·|_∞` and the `|·|ₚ`: the *places* of ℚ are the primes together with one infinite place. This
file contains the analytic heart of his argument, the **digit bound**: for integers `m, n ≥ 2`
and any absolute value `φ`,

  `log φ(m) · log n ≤ log m · log max(1, φ(n))`.

The proof writes `m^k` in base `n`. It has about `k · log m / log n` digits, each digit `r < n`
has `φ(r) ≤ r < n`, and so `φ(m)^k ≤ (#digits) · n · max(1, φ(n))^(#digits)`. Taking logarithms,
dividing by `k`, and letting `k → ∞` kills the factor `#digits`, which grows only linearly in `k`
(we let `k = t²` run through the squares, so that `log k = 2 log t ≤ 2t` is visibly `o(k)`).

The bound is stated for any `B ≥ max(1, φ(n))`; it is used in `Ostrowski` with `B = 1` and with
`B = φ(n)`.

# Ostrowski's theorem, II: the classification

**Ostrowski's theorem** (1916): every nontrivial absolute value on ℚ is equivalent to the
ordinary absolute value `|·|_∞` or to the `p`-adic absolute value `|·|ₚ` for exactly one
prime `p`.

So the *completions* of ℚ — the fields in which Cauchy sequences for some absolute value converge
— are ℝ and the fields ℚₚ, and nothing else. This is why number theory speaks of the *places*
`2, 3, 5, 7, …, ∞` of ℚ, and why the local–global principle (Hasse, 1921: a quadratic form over
ℚ represents `0` iff it does so over ℝ and over every ℚₚ) quantifies over exactly these fields.
In the Langlands programme the same list reappears: the adèle ring of ℚ is a restricted product
over all places, automorphic representations factor as tensor products of local representations,
one at each place, and the *local* Langlands correspondence is a statement about each ℚₚ and ℝ
separately.

The proof splits according to the dichotomy supplied by the digit bound of `OstrowskiBound`:

* **Archimedean case.** If `φ(n₀) > 1` for some natural `n₀`, then `φ(n) > 1` for every `n ≥ 2`,
  and the digit bound applied in both directions gives `log φ(m) / log m = log φ(n) / log n`;
  calling the common value `s`, we get `φ = |·|_∞^s`.
* **Non-archimedean case.** If `φ(n) ≤ 1` for all naturals `n`, some prime `p` has `φ(p) < 1`
  (otherwise `φ` would be trivial), and no other prime `q` can: from Bézout,
  `1 = a pᵏ + b qᵏ` would give `1 ≤ φ(p)ᵏ + φ(q)ᵏ < 1` for large `k`. Unique factorisation then
  gives `φ(x) = φ(p)^(vₚ(x))`, i.e. `φ = |·|ₚ^s` with `s = −log φ(p) / log p`.

# The `p`-adic integers ℤₚ

Hensel's `p`-adic integers are "integers written in base `p` with infinitely many digits to the
left", such as `… 2 2 2 3` in base `7`. A cleaner description: a `p`-adic integer is a
*compatible system of residues* — a residue class mod `p`, one mod `p²`, one mod `p³`, … — each
reducing to the previous one. That is, ℤₚ is the inverse limit `lim ℤ/pⁿ`.

We realise this with a quotient, the same device that built ℤ, ℚ and ℝ. A **`p`-adic sequence**
is a sequence of integers `x₀, x₁, x₂, …` with `pⁿ ∣ xₙ₊₁ − xₙ` (so `xₙ` is meaningful mod `pⁿ`),
and two such sequences are identified when `pⁿ ∣ xₙ − yₙ` for every `n`. Addition and
multiplication are done term by term — no reductions needed — so every ring law of ℤ passes
straight to ℤₚ. In the language of `Valuation`, a `p`-adic sequence is a Cauchy sequence of
integers for `|·|ₚ` with a prescribed rate (`|xₙ₊₁ − xₙ|ₚ ≤ p^(−n)`), and identified sequences
are those whose difference tends to `0` at that rate: informally, ℤₚ is the completion of ℤ
(this identification is explained here, not formalised).

We prove that ℤₚ is a commutative ring (registered with `grind`), that ℤ embeds in it, define
congruence modulo `pᵏ` on ℤₚ, and prove the *completeness* of ℤₚ in its natural form: every
sequence of `p`-adic integers that is Cauchy modulo powers of `p` converges. The next file uses
this ring for Hensel's lemma.
