# `σ_q` is the Frobenius at `q`, for every `n ≥ 1`

This file extends `Frobenius.lean` from prime `p` to arbitrary `n ≥ 1`, using the integer
cyclotomic polynomial `Φ_n = cycloZ n` of `IrreducibleN.lean`.

* **The ring `ℤ[ζ_n]`** is the image of evaluation `ℤ[x] → ℂ`, `f ↦ f(ζ_n)` (`intZeta n`, as in
  `Frobenius.lean`). It lies in `ℚ(ζ_n)`.
* **The kernel of evaluation** consists of the integer multiples of `Φ_n`
  (`dvd_cycloZ_of_evZeta`). `Φ_n` is monic with integer coefficients and is the minimal
  polynomial of `ζ_n` over `ℚ`, so `Φ_n ∣ f` over `ℚ` and then over `ℤ`.
* **Reduction modulo `q`.** Hence `f(ζ_n) ↦ f mod (q, Φ_n)` is a well-defined ring homomorphism
  `ℤ[ζ_n] → A_n = 𝔽_q[x]/(Φ̄_n)` with `ζ_n ↦ x` (`reduceN`). The ring `A_n` is not zero,
  because `Φ̄_n` is monic of degree `φ(n) ≥ 1` (`resRingN_nontrivial`).
* **Frobenius.** For a prime `q ∤ n` and `α = f(ζ_n)`, `σ_q(α) = f(ζ_n^q)` reduces to
  `f̄(x^q) = f̄(x)^q`. So **`σ_q(α) ≡ α^q (mod q)`** for every `α ∈ ℤ[ζ_n]`
  (`reduceN_galAut`).

As in `Frobenius.lean`, we do not prove that `A_n ≅ ℤ[ζ_n]/(q)`.

# The `GL(1)` dictionary over `ℚ(ζ_n)`: Dirichlet characters are Galois characters

This file states the abelian case of the Langlands correspondence over `ℚ` in its most classical
form, for the cyclotomic field `ℚ(ζ_n)` and every `n ≥ 1`.

**The two sides.** On the *automorphic* side of `GL(1)` over `ℚ` stand the Dirichlet characters
modulo `n`, i.e. the characters `χ : (ℤ/n)ˣ → ℂ` (`Character (ZModUnits n)`). (In general one has
Hecke characters, i.e. characters of the idèle class group; over `ℚ` the Hecke characters of
finite order are exactly the Dirichlet characters, but that identification is not formalised
here.) On the *Galois* side stand the one-dimensional representations of the Galois group, here
the characters `ρ : Gal(ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ) → ℂ` (`Character (FieldAut Qc (cycloFieldN hn))`). A
character of a finite group takes values in the unit circle, so this is the same as a
homomorphism into `ℂˣ`.

**The dictionary.** Transporting characters along `cycloGaloisIsoN : (ℤ/n)ˣ ≅ Gal(ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ)`
gives an isomorphism of groups of characters (`dirichletGaloisN`), and the defining property of
the dictionary is the match at Frobenius elements: for a prime `q ∤ n`,

  `ρ_χ(σ_q) = χ(q)`   (`dirichletGaloisN_frobenius`),

where `σ_q : ζ_n ↦ ζ_n^q` is the automorphism shown to reduce to the `q`-th power map modulo `q`
in `FrobeniusN.lean` (`reduceN_galAut`). This is what makes the Artin `L`-function
`L(s, ρ_χ) = ∏_q (1 - ρ_χ(Frob_q) q^{-s})⁻¹` and the Dirichlet `L`-function
`L(s, χ) = ∏_q (1 - χ(q) q^{-s})⁻¹` have the same Euler factors at the unramified primes; see
`EulerFactors.lean`.

**Frobenius elements fill the group.** Using Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions
(`Foundations.NumberTheory.dirichlet`), every element of `Gal(ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ)` is `σ_q` for
infinitely many primes `q` (`exists_frobenius_eq`), a qualitative form of the Chebotarev
density theorem for `ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ`. Hence a Galois character is determined by its values at the
Frobenius elements, and `ρ_χ` is the *unique* Galois character with `ρ(σ_q) = χ(q)` for all primes
`q ∤ n` (`dirichletGaloisN_unique`).

**What is not claimed.** This is `GL(1)` Langlands for the single abelian extension `ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ`.
The passage to all abelian extensions of `ℚ` needs the Kronecker–Weber theorem, and the passage
to other base fields needs class field theory; neither is formalised. Prime ideals of `ℤ[ζ_n]`
are not formalised either: "Frobenius at `q`" always means the automorphism `σ_q` together with
the congruence `σ_q(α) ≡ α^q (mod q)` on `ℤ[ζ_n]`.

# Euler factors: Dirichlet `L`-functions and Artin `L`-functions over `ℚ(ζ_n)`

An **`L`-function** packages arithmetic data prime by prime into an Euler product.

* **Dirichlet** (1837), for a Dirichlet character `χ` modulo `n`:
  `L(s, χ) = Σ χ(m) m^{-s} = ∏_q (1 - χ(q) q^{-s})⁻¹`. The coefficient at `q` is `χ(q)`, which is
  `0` for `q ∣ n`. Hecke (1918) extended this to characters of idèle class groups of number
  fields, the automorphic objects of `GL(1)`.
* **Artin** (1923, 1930), for a representation `ρ` of `Gal(K/ℚ)`: at an unramified prime `q` the
  Euler factor is `det(1 - ρ(Frob_q) q^{-s})⁻¹`. For a character `ρ` this is
  `(1 - ρ(Frob_q) q^{-s})⁻¹`. (At ramified primes Artin uses the inertia invariants; we do not
  formalise inertia groups, and treat only the unramified primes, i.e. `q ∤ n` for
  `K = ℚ(ζ_n)`.)

`GL(1)` Langlands over `ℚ` says that every Artin `L`-function of a Galois character is a
Dirichlet `L`-function, factor by factor. For `ℚ(ζ_n)` this is formal once the dictionary
`χ ↔ ρ_χ` of `DictionaryN.lean` is known, since `ρ_χ(σ_q) = χ(q)` for primes `q ∤ n`:

* the local factors agree at every prime `q ∤ n` (`localFactor_match`);
* the finite partial Euler products agree: the Dirichlet product over *all* primes `q < N` equals
  the Artin product over the unramified primes `q < N` (`dirichletEuler_eq_artinEuler`), because
  the Dirichlet factors at `q ∣ n` are `(1 - 0)⁻¹ = 1`.

These are identities between finite products in `ℂ`, for every natural exponent `s` (the
interesting range being `s ≥ 2`, where the infinite products converge absolutely). **Nothing is
claimed about the analytic `L`-functions** themselves: no convergence, no limits, no analytic
continuation. Note also that for an imprimitive `χ` the Dirichlet factor at a prime `q ∣ n`
is `1`, while the full Artin factor there need not be; this is why the comparison is made on
the unramified primes.

# Frobenius in the quadratic subfield `ℚ(√p*)`: the Galois side of splitting

For an odd prime `p` the cyclotomic field `ℚ(ζ_p)` contains exactly one quadratic field,
`ℚ(√p*)` with `p* = (-1)^((p-1)/2) p` (`Quadratic.lean`, `QuadraticFixed.lean`). For a prime
`q ≠ p`, the restriction of the Frobenius `σ_q` to `ℚ(√p*)` is either the identity or the
non-trivial automorphism `√p* ↦ -√p*`. In the language of prime ideals, `q` *splits* in
`ℚ(√p*)` exactly when this restriction is trivial, and is *inert* otherwise; and, for odd `q`,
`q` splits exactly when `p*` is a square modulo `q`.

**Prime ideals are not formalised in this library.** We therefore state everything through
Frobenius: "`q` splits in `ℚ(√p*)`" is replaced by "`σ_q` fixes `ℚ(√p*)` pointwise", where
`σ_q : ζ_p ↦ ζ_p^q` is the automorphism shown to reduce to the `q`-th power map modulo `q` in
`Frobenius.lean`. The identification of this condition with splitting of the prime ideal `(q)`
is classical but is **not** proved here.

The two descriptions of the condition are:

* **Galois side, read in `(ℤ/p)ˣ`.** `σ_q` fixes `ℚ(√p*)` iff `q` is a square mod `p`, i.e.
  `(q/p) = 1` (`galAut_fixes_sqrtField_iff`): `ℚ(√p*)` is the fixed field of the squares.
* **Arithmetic side, read modulo `q`.** By Gauss's congruence `(q/p) ≡ (p*)^((q-1)/2) (mod q)`
  (`legendre_eq_pstar_pow_mod`, which is quadratic reciprocity) and Euler's criterion modulo `q`,
  `(q/p) = 1` iff `p*` is a square modulo `q`.

Together (`frobenius_fixes_sqrtField_iff_pstar_sq`): **`σ_q` fixes `ℚ(√p*)` iff `p*` is a square
modulo `q`**, for distinct odd primes `p, q`. This is the decomposition law of the quadratic field
`ℚ(√p*)`, phrased via Frobenius. In the language of the `GL(1)` dictionary (said here in prose
only): the quadratic character `(·/p)` of `(ℤ/p)ˣ` corresponds to the character of
`Gal(ℚ(ζ_p)/ℚ)` whose kernel is the subgroup fixing `ℚ(√p*)`, and its value at `σ_q` is `(q/p)`.
The prime `q = 2` is excluded: every integer is a square modulo
`2`, while `2` splits in `ℚ(√p*)` only when `p* ≡ 1 (mod 8)`.

# Part XV, chapter 3: reciprocity as Galois theory (the cyclotomic case)

The Langlands programme predicts a correspondence between Galois representations and
automorphic forms. For `GL(1)`, i.e. one-dimensional representations, the prediction is class
field theory, and over `ℚ` its prototype is the cyclotomic field `ℚ(ζ_p)`. This chapter
formalises that prototype.

* **Gauss, 1801.** In the *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* Gauss proved that `Φ_p = 1 + x + ⋯ +
  x^{p-1}` is irreducible over `ℚ`, studied the periods of `p`-th roots of unity, and showed
  that the quadratic Gauss sum `g = Σ (a/p) ζ^a` satisfies `g² = ±p`. Here: `Φ_p` is
  irreducible via Eisenstein's criterion applied to `Φ_p(x + 1)` (`cyclo_irreducible`), and
  `g² = p* = (-1)^((p-1)/2) p` holds in any commutative ring containing a suitable `p`-th root
  of unity (`gaussSum_sq`), in particular in `ℂ` (`gaussSum_sq_complex`). So `√p* ∈ ℚ(ζ_p)`
  (`sqrt_pstar_mem`).
* **Galois.** `Aut(ℚ(ζ_p)/ℚ) ≅ (ℤ/p)ˣ`, with `a` acting by `ζ ↦ ζ^a` (`cycloGaloisIso`). The
  group is abelian, and `[ℚ(ζ_p) : ℚ] = p - 1` (`deg_cycloField`): the powers
  `1, ζ_p, …, ζ_p^{p-2}` form a basis.
* **Frobenius.** `σ_q` is defined as `ζ ↦ ζ^q`. On `ℤ[ζ_p] ⊆ ℚ(ζ_p)` (`intZeta`) there is a
  reduction homomorphism to `𝔽_q[x]/(Φ_p)` sending `ζ_p` to `x` (`reduce`), and
  `σ_q(α) ≡ α^q` for every `α ∈ ℤ[ζ_p]` (`reduce_galAut`). So `σ_q` is a genuine Frobenius
  element at `q`. The Gauss sum reduces to the Gauss sum modulo `q` (`reduce_gaussSum`).
* **The quadratic subfield.** `σ_a` fixes `ℚ(√p*)` exactly when `a` is a square mod `p`
  (`galAut_fixes_sqrtField_iff`), `√p*` is irrational (`gaussSum_not_rat`),
  `[ℚ(√p*) : ℚ] = 2` (`deg_sqrtField`), and the fixed field of the squares is `ℚ(√p*)`
  (`fixedField_squares`).
* **Gauss, 1808.** The sixth proof of quadratic reciprocity: in the characteristic-`q` ring
  `𝔽_q[x]/(Φ_p)`, Frobenius gives `g^q = (q/p) g`, while `g² = p*` gives
  `g^q = (p*)^((q-1)/2) g`. Hence `(q/p) ≡ (p*)^((q-1)/2) (mod q)`
  (`legendre_eq_pstar_pow_mod`) and the law of quadratic reciprocity
  (`quadratic_reciprocity_gauss`). In ℂ the same phenomenon reads `σ_a(√p*) = (a/p)√p*`, so the
  Frobenius automorphism `σ_q` fixes `√p*` exactly when `p*` is a square modulo `q`
  (`frobenius_fixes_sqrt_iff`).
* **Prime powers.** For `n = p^{k+1}`, `Φ_n = Σ_{j<p} x^{j p^k}` is irreducible over `ℚ`
  (`cycloPP_irreducible`, Eisenstein at `p` after `x ↦ x + 1`, using `Φ_n(x+1) ≡ x^{φ(n)}`
  mod `p`), `Aut(ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ) ≅ (ℤ/n)ˣ` (`cycloGaloisIsoPP`), and `[ℚ(ζ_n) : ℚ] = (p - 1)p^k`
  (`deg_cycloFieldPP`).
* **General `n` (Kronecker 1854, Dedekind 1857).** For every `n ≥ 1`,
  `Φ_n = ∏_{a < n, gcd(a,n) = 1} (x - ζ_n^a)` is defined over `ℂ` (`cycloC`), has degree
  `φ(n)` (`natDegree_cycloC`), and is the image of a monic integer polynomial `cycloZ n` of
  degree `φ(n)` (`map_cycloZ`, `natDegree_cycloZ`). It is irreducible over `ℚ`
  (`cycloQ_irreducible`) and is the minimal polynomial of `ζ_n` (`aeval_zetaN_eq_zero_iff`);
  for prime `p` it is the earlier `Φ_p` (`cycloQ_prime`). The proof is Dedekind's: for a prime
  `p ∤ n`, `ζ ↦ ζ^p` preserves the minimal polynomial (`dedekind_step`), by Gauss's lemma for
  monic factors (`int_of_monic_factor`) and the separability of `xⁿ - 1` modulo `p`
  (`isUnit_of_sq_dvd_X_pow_sub_one`). Consequently `Aut(ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ) ≅ (ℤ/n)ˣ`
  (`cycloGaloisIsoN`), `[ℚ(ζ_n) : ℚ] = φ(n)` (`deg_cycloFieldN`), and for every prime `q ∤ n`
  the automorphism `σ_q` reduces to the `q`-th power map `ℤ[ζ_n] → 𝔽_q[x]/(Φ̄_n)`
  (`reduceN_galAut`).
* **Kummer** (1840s) made `ℤ[ζ_p]` the object of an arithmetic of ideal numbers. We use it only
  through its reduction map to `𝔽_q[x]/(Φ_p)`. We do not prove that this ring is
  `ℤ[ζ_p]/(q)`, nor anything about ideals of `ℤ[ζ_p]`.
* **Kronecker–Weber** (Kronecker 1853; Weber 1886; Hilbert 1896): every finite abelian
  extension of `ℚ` lies in a cyclotomic field. *Stated here in prose only; not formalised.*
* **Artin reciprocity** (1927): for an abelian extension, Frobenius elements depend only on the
  prime modulo the conductor, and characters of the Galois group correspond to characters of
  idèle class groups. In the cyclotomic case, one ingredient is the (proved) fact that `σ_q` depends
  only on `q mod n` (`frobN_congr`); Artin reciprocity itself is not formalised. For prime `p`, a Dirichlet character `χ` mod `p`, transported to `Gal(ℚ(ζ_p)/ℚ)`,
  takes the value `χ(q)` at the Frobenius element `σ_q` (`galChar_frobenius`).
* **The `GL(1)` dictionary for every `n ≥ 1`.** The characters of a commutative group form a
  commutative group (`characterCommGroup`), `Gal(ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ)` is a finite abelian group of order
  `φ(n)` (`card_cycloGaloisN`), and transport along `cycloGaloisIsoN` is a group isomorphism
  `χ ↦ ρ_χ` from Dirichlet characters mod `n` to characters of `Gal(ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ)`
  (`dirichletGaloisN`) with `ρ_χ(σ_q) = χ(q)` for every prime `q ∤ n`

  Galois element is `σ_q` for infinitely many primes `q` (`exists_frobenius_eq`, a qualitative
  cyclotomic Chebotarev), so `ρ_χ` is the unique Galois character with these Frobenius values
  (`dirichletGaloisN_unique`).
* **Euler factors.** Consequently the local factors `(1 - χ(q) q^{-s})⁻¹` of the Dirichlet

  `q ∤ n` (`localFactor_match`), and the finite partial Euler products agree
  (`dirichletEuler_eq_artinEuler`). These are identities of finite products in `ℂ`; nothing is
  claimed about analytic `L`-functions.
* **Splitting in `ℚ(√p*)`, via Frobenius.** For distinct odd primes `p, q`, the Frobenius `σ_q`

  being quadratic reciprocity. This is the Galois-side form of "`q` splits in `ℚ(√p*)`"; prime
  ideals are not formalised, so splitting itself is not stated.
* **Langlands for `GL(1)`** is this correspondence between Galois characters and Dirichlet
  (more generally Hecke) characters. Langlands' conjectures (1967) extend it to `GL(n)`. Beyond

  characters of `ℚ` with Dirichlet characters, and the analytic theory of Artin `L`-functions are

# Composition identities for sums of squares

Diophantus of Alexandria (*Arithmetica* III.19, c. 250 AD) already knew that the product of
two sums of two squares is again a sum of two squares: `65 = 5 · 13 = 1² + 8² = 4² + 7²`.
In modern terms this is the multiplicativity of the norm on the Gaussian integers, and it
was written down as an algebraic identity by Brahmagupta (628) and by Fibonacci (1225):

  `(a² + b²)(c² + d²) = (ac − bd)² + (ad + bc)²`.

Euler, in a letter to Goldbach of 4 May 1748, found the analogous identity for **four**
squares — the multiplicativity of the norm on Hamilton's quaternions, a century before
quaternions existed. Both identities are the reason why the question "which numbers are sums
of `k` squares?" reduces, for `k = 2` and `k = 4`, to the question for primes. (For three
squares there is no such identity; this is one reason the three-square theorem is so much
harder: `3 = 1² + 1² + 1²` and `5 = 2² + 1² + 0²` are sums of three squares, but `15 = 3 · 5` is
not.)

This file proves both identities over `ℤ` (by `grind`'s ring normaliser), packages them as
closure properties of the predicates `IsSum2` and `IsSum4`, and bridges between integer and
natural-number representations (`a² = |a|²`).

# Lagrange's four-square theorem

Diophantus seems to have assumed, without comment, that every number is a sum of four squares
(in problems of Book IV of the *Arithmetica*), and Bachet stated it explicitly in his 1621
edition. Fermat claimed a
proof by infinite descent but never published one. Euler worked on it for forty years: he found
the four-square identity (1748, see `Identities`) and showed that `x² + y² + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p)` is
always solvable, but could not close the descent. Lagrange did, in 1770, explicitly building on
Euler's work; Euler soon gave a simpler version of the descent. We follow that classical route.

1. **Euler's congruence** (`exists_sq_add_sq_add_one`). For an odd prime `p` the `(p + 1)/2`
   values `x² mod p` (`0 ≤ x ≤ (p − 1)/2`) are distinct, and so are the `(p + 1)/2` values
   `−1 − y² mod p`; as `p + 1 > p`, the pigeonhole principle forces a coincidence between the two
   families, i.e. `x² + y² + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p)`. Hence `m₀ p = x² + y² + 1² + 0²` with `0 < m₀ < p`.
2. **Descent** (`descent`). If `m p` is a sum of four squares with `1 < m < p`, so is `r p` for
   some `0 < r < m`: reduce the four numbers modulo `m` into `(−m/2, m/2]`, write the sum of the
   residues' squares as `m r`, and divide the Euler product `(m p)(m r)` by `m²`. The two
   degenerate cases `r = 0` and `r = m` would make `m` divide `p`.
3. **Lagrange's theorem** (`lagrange_four_squares`) follows from the prime case by Euler's
   identity and induction on the number of prime factors.

# Three squares: the necessary condition

That numbers of the form `8b + 7` are never sums of three squares was known in the seventeenth
century (it is stated by Descartes and by Fermat), and **Legendre** (*Essai sur la théorie des nombres*, 1798) stated the full theorem, with a proof resting on the then-unproved Dirichlet theorem:

> a natural number is a sum of three squares if and only if it is not of the form `4ᵃ(8b + 7)`.

Legendre's proof of sufficiency had a gap (it used Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions
before Dirichlet proved it); **Gauss** gave a complete proof in the *Disquisitiones* (1801, art. 291–292),
via his theory of ternary quadratic forms, and also counted the representations in terms of class
numbers of binary forms. The easy half, formalised here, is a congruence argument:

* a square is `≡ 0, 1` or `4 (mod 8)`, so a sum of three squares is never `≡ 7 (mod 8)`;
* if `x² + y² + z² ≡ 0 (mod 4)` then `x, y, z` are all even (odd squares are `≡ 1 (mod 4)`), so
  `4ᵃ⁺¹(8b + 7)` is a sum of three squares only if `4ᵃ(8b + 7)` is.

In the language of the Hasse principle, `8b + 7` is the obstruction at the prime `2`: the form
`x² + y² + z²` does not represent `7` over `ℚ₂`. The sufficiency direction (every other number *is*
a sum of three squares) is the content of `ThreeSquaresSuff`, which combines both halves into
`three_squares_iff`.

# Which numbers are sums of two squares?

Fermat's Christmas-day letter of 1640 contained more than the theorem on primes `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)`
(`Foundations.Algebra.fermat_two_squares`, Zagier's proof). Fermat also knew the complete
answer, made rigorous by Euler (1749–1758): a positive integer `n` is a sum of two squares if and
only if every prime `p ≡ 3 (mod 4)` divides `n` to an **even** power. Thus `45 = 3² · 5 = 6² + 3²`,
but `21 = 3 · 7` and `12 = 2² · 3` are not sums of two squares.

* **Sufficiency** is multiplicative: `2 = 1² + 1²`, primes `≡ 1 (mod 4)` are sums of two squares
  by Fermat, `p² = p² + 0²`, and the Brahmagupta identity multiplies representations.
* **Necessity** is a divisibility argument: if `p ≡ 3 (mod 4)` divides `a² + b²` then `p` divides
  both `a` and `b`, since otherwise `(b a⁻¹)² ≡ −1 (mod p)`, contradicting Fermat's criterion
  `neg_one_qr_iff` (the first supplement to quadratic reciprocity). Dividing by `p²` lowers the
  exponent of `p` by two, and an odd exponent eventually reaches `1`, which is impossible.

We phrase "`p` occurs to the exact power `k`" without a valuation function: `pᵏ ∣ n` and
`pᵏ⁺¹ ∤ n`. For `n = 0` the condition is vacuous, consistently with `0 = 0² + 0²`.

# The Davenport–Cassels lemma for three squares

If a number is a sum of three *rational* squares, is it a sum of three *integer* squares? For the
form `x² + y² + z²` the answer is yes, by a beautiful geometric descent usually attributed to
Davenport and Cassels (it is the route taken in Serre's *Cours d'arithmétique*, 1970), although
the argument was found earlier by L. Aubry (1912).

Write the rational point as `X / t` with `X ∈ ℤ³`, `t ≥ 1`, `|X|² = k t²`. Round it to the nearest
lattice point `Y`, so every coordinate of `X − tY` is at most `t/2` in absolute value, hence
`|X − tY|² ≤ 3t²/4 < t²`. If `X = tY` we are done. Otherwise the line through `Y` and `X / t`
meets the sphere `|v|² = k` in a second rational point, and a short computation shows that its
denominator is

  `t' = |X − tY|² / t = k t − 2 X·Y + t |Y|²`, with `0 < t' < t`;

the new numerator is `X' = t' Y + (|Y|² − k)(X − tY)`, and `|X'|² = k t'²` is a polynomial
identity. Strong induction on `t` finishes the proof (`davenport_cassels`).

The Euclidean property used here — every point of `ℚ³` is at squared distance `< 1` from a point
of `ℤ³` — is what the lemma needs in general; it holds for sums of two, three or four squares but
fails for most positive forms, for which rational and integral representability differ.

# Legendre symbols of odd numbers modulo a prime

The sufficiency proof of the three-square theorem (`ThreeSquaresSuff`) chooses an auxiliary prime
`q ≡ 1 (mod 4)` by Dirichlet's theorem and then needs to know that a given squarefree `k` is a
square modulo `q`. By quadratic reciprocity, `(p/q) = (q/p)` for every odd prime `p ∣ k`, and the
right-hand side is controlled by the residue of `q` modulo `p`. Multiplying over the prime factors
of `k` produces the value of a *character of `k` modulo 4 or 8*:

* if `q ≡ −1 (mod p)` then `(p/q) = (−1/p) = χ₄(p)`, so `(k/q) = χ₄(k)`, where
  `χ₄(m) = ±1` according as `m ≡ ±1 (mod 4)`;
* if `2q ≡ −1 (mod p)` then `(p/q) = (−2/p) = χ₈(p)`, so `(k/q) = χ₈(k)`, where
  `χ₈(m) = 1` exactly for `m ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8)`.

This is the Jacobi-symbol calculus in the special case needed, without defining the Jacobi
symbol: `legendre_eq_char` is the multiplicativity statement that a completely multiplicative
`χ` (on odd numbers) agreeing with `(·/q)` at all prime factors of `m` agrees at `m`. It is the
point at which Legendre's `4ᵃ(8b + 7)` condition enters: `χ₄(k) = 1` for `k ≡ 1 (mod 4)` and
`χ₈(k) = 1` for `k ≡ 3 (mod 8)`, but neither helps for `k ≡ 7 (mod 8)`.

# Three squares: sufficiency (Legendre 1798, Gauss 1801)

Every natural number that is not of the form `4ᵃ(8b + 7)` is a sum of three squares. Legendre
stated this in 1798; his argument assumed that suitable arithmetic progressions contain primes,
which Dirichlet proved only in 1837. Gauss gave the first complete proof (*Disquisitiones*, art. 291–292)
through his reduction theory of ternary forms. The proof formalised here is a modern hybrid, in
the spirit of the treatment in Serre's *Cours d'arithmétique*, but with the Hasse–Minkowski
theorem for the quaternary form `x² + y² + z² − k t²` replaced by **Legendre's theorem on
conics** (`Padic.Legendre.legendre_sufficient`) and **Dirichlet's theorem**
(`NumberTheory.dirichlet`), all of which this library already proves:

1. *Reduction to squarefree `k`.* Remove factors of `4`, and write what remains as `s² k` with `k`
   squarefree; then `s` is odd and `k ≡ 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 (mod 8)`.
2. *An auxiliary prime.* By Dirichlet, choose a prime `q > k`, `q ≡ 1 (mod 4)`, in a residue
   class modulo `4k` arranged so that `q ≡ −1 (mod k)` (if `k ≢ 3 mod 8`) or `2q ≡ −1 (mod k)`
   (if `k ≡ 3 mod 8`). Quadratic reciprocity (`Symbols`) then shows that `k` is a square
   modulo `q`; this is where `k ≢ 7 (mod 8)` is used.
3. *A conic.* With `b = q` or `b = 2q`, Legendre's conditions hold for `x² + b y² − k z² = 0`,
   which therefore has a non-trivial integer point, necessarily with `z ≠ 0`. As `b` is a sum of
   two squares (Fermat), `k z²` is a sum of three integer squares.
4. *Clearing the denominator.* By the Davenport–Cassels lemma (`DavenportCassels`), `k` itself is a
   sum of three integer squares.

# Sums of squares

Which numbers are sums of `k` squares? The question is as old as number theory, and it is the
prototype of the arithmetic of quadratic forms: the form `x₁² + ⋯ + x_k²` is the simplest positive
definite form, and asking which integers it represents is asking for its *values*.

**Diophantus** (*Arithmetica*, c. 250 AD) knew that a product of sums of two squares is a sum of
two squares, and seems to have taken for granted that every number is a sum of four squares.
**Fermat** (1640) announced that the primes `≡ 1 (mod 4)` are sums of two squares, gave the
complete answer for two squares, and claimed the four-square theorem by descent, without
publishing proofs. **Euler** proved the two-square results (1749–58), found the four-square
identity (1748) and the congruence `x² + y² + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p)`, but not the descent; **Lagrange**
completed the four-square theorem in 1770. For three squares, **Legendre** (1798) stated and
nearly proved that `n` is a sum of three squares iff `n ≠ 4ᵃ(8b + 7)`; **Gauss** (1801) gave the
first complete proof via ternary quadratic forms.

## What this sub-part proves

* `Identities` — Brahmagupta's two-square and **Euler's four-square identity**
  (`euler_four_square_identity`), packaged as closure of `IsSum2` and `IsSum4` under products.
* `FourSquares` — **Lagrange's four-square theorem** (`lagrange_four_squares`): every natural
  number is a sum of four squares. Euler's congruence by pigeonhole, then Lagrange's descent.
* `ThreeSquares` — the **necessary condition** in Legendre's three-square theorem
  (`not_sum_three_squares`): no `4ᵃ(8b + 7)` is a sum of three squares (a congruence mod 8).
* `TwoSquares` — the **two-squares theorem** (`two_squares_iff`): `n` is a sum of two squares
  iff every prime `p ≡ 3 (mod 4)` divides `n` to an even exact power. Sufficiency uses Fermat's
  theorem `Foundations.Algebra.fermat_two_squares` (Zagier's proof) and Brahmagupta's identity;
  necessity uses Fermat's criterion for `−1` (`Foundations.Algebra.neg_one_qr_iff`).
* `DavenportCassels` — the **Davenport–Cassels lemma** for `x² + y² + z²` (`davenport_cassels`):

* `Symbols` — the Legendre-symbol computations needed below: `(k/q) = χ₄(k)` or `χ₈(k)` for odd

## Representation numbers, and the road to modular forms

Beyond *whether* `n` is a sum of `k` squares one can ask *in how many ways*: let `r_k(n)` count the
integer vectors `(x₁, …, x_k)` with `x₁² + ⋯ + x_k² = n` (signs and order counted). Then
`r₂(n) = 4 (d₁(n) − d₃(n))`, where `d_i(n)` counts the divisors of `n` that are `≡ i (mod 4)`
(a formula found by Jacobi, and implicit in Gauss), and **Jacobi's four-square formula** reads
`r₄(n) = 8 · Σ_{d ∣ n, 4 ∤ d} d`, which is positive for every `n ≥ 1` and so re-proves Lagrange.
Gauss expressed `r₃(n)` through class numbers of binary quadratic forms. Jacobi found these
formulas by studying the theta series `θ(q) = Σ_{x ∈ ℤ} q^{x²}`, whose `k`-th power is
`Σ_n r_k(n) qⁿ`: in modern language `θ(τ)^k` is a **modular form** of weight `k/2` for the group
`Γ₀(4)`, and the divisor-sum formulas say that for `k = 4` it equals an Eisenstein series. That is
the bridge from sums of squares to modular forms, and through them to the automorphic side of
the Langlands programme. None of this — `r_k`, the formulas of Jacobi and Gauss, theta series,
modular forms — is formalised here; it is recorded only as the direction in which the subject
continues.

# The modular group SL₂(ℤ)

In 1877–1880 Felix Klein and, independently and from a different direction, Henri Poincaré
put a single group at the centre of nineteenth-century analysis: the group of integer
`2 × 2` matrices of determinant one,

  `SL₂(ℤ) = { (a b; c d) : a, b, c, d ∈ ℤ, ad − bc = 1 }`.

Klein met it through the icosahedron, elliptic modular functions and the "modular
figure" (the tessellation of the upper half-plane by copies of a curvilinear triangle);
Poincaré met it through Fuchsian functions and recognised that its action on the upper
half-plane is an action by isometries of the hyperbolic plane. Both saw that the functions
invariant (or nearly invariant) under this group — *modular functions* and *modular forms* —
carry arithmetic information: Jacobi's theta functions, Eisenstein series, the `j`-invariant
classifying elliptic curves.

This file builds the group itself, from Lean's built-in integers. A matrix is a structure
with four integer entries and a proof that the determinant is `1`; multiplication is the
usual matrix product (the determinant is multiplicative), and the inverse of `(a b; c d)` is
`(d −b; −c a)`. We register it as a `Group` in the sense of `Foundations.Algebra.Group`.

We then define the two classical generators

  `S = (0 −1; 1 0)`  (the inversion `τ ↦ −1/τ`),  `T = (1 1; 0 1)`  (the translation `τ ↦ τ + 1`),

and verify the defining relations of the modular group: `S² = −I` and `(ST)³ = −I`. (That
these relations, together with `−I` being central of order two, give a *presentation* of
`SL₂(ℤ)` is a classical theorem not proved here; the file `Generation` proves the weaker
statement that `S` and `T` generate.)

# SL₂(ℤ) acting on the upper half-plane

The **upper half-plane** is `ℍ = { τ ∈ ℂ : Im τ > 0 }`. A matrix `γ = (a b; c d)` of
determinant one acts on it by the **Möbius transformation**

  `γ τ = (a τ + b) / (c τ + d)`.

Poincaré's insight (1882) was that ℍ, with the metric `|dτ|² / (Im τ)²`, is a model of the
hyperbolic plane of Bolyai and Lobachevsky, and that these transformations are exactly its
orientation-preserving isometries (for real matrices). We do not formalise the metric; we
prove the algebraic heart of the matter, the imaginary-part formula

  `Im (γ τ) = Im τ / |c τ + d|²`  (`im_mob`, valid because `ad − bc = 1`),

from which it follows that `γ` maps ℍ into ℍ. We then show that this is a **group action**
of SL₂(ℤ) on ℍ (`instMulAction`: `I τ = τ` and `(γδ) τ = γ (δ τ)`), using the
**cocycle identity** for the automorphy factor `j(γ, τ) = c τ + d`,

  `j(γδ, τ) = j(γ, δτ) · j(δ, τ)`  (`denom_mul`),

which is also exactly what makes the definition of a modular form of weight `k`
(`f(γτ) = j(γ, τ)^k f(τ)`, file `Forms`) consistent. Finally `−I` acts trivially
(`negOne_smul`), so the action factors through `PSL₂(ℤ) = SL₂(ℤ)/{±I}`.

The complex numbers `C` and the reals `R` are the from-scratch constructions of Part II;
integer matrix entries enter through the canonical casts `ℤ → ℝ → ℂ`.

# The fundamental domain of SL₂(ℤ)

Gauss already knew, in the language of binary quadratic forms (*Disquisitiones*, 1801), that
every positive definite form is equivalent to a *reduced* one. Translated into the action of
SL₂(ℤ) on the upper half-plane by Dedekind (1877) and Klein (1879), this becomes the
statement that the curvilinear triangle

  `F = { τ ∈ ℍ : |Re τ| ≤ 1/2, |τ| ≥ 1 }`

meets every orbit: Klein's "modular figure" is the tessellation of ℍ by the images `γF`.
Poincaré turned such fundamental polygons into the main tool for constructing automorphic
functions for arbitrary Fuchsian groups.

## The argument formalised here (`exists_mem_F`)

Fix `τ = x + iy ∈ ℍ`. By `Action.im_mob`, `Im (γτ) = y / |cτ + d|²`, so making `Im` large
means making `|cτ + d|² = (cx + d)² + (cy)²` small.

1. **Finiteness** (`bounds`). If `|cτ + d|² ≤ 1` then `|cy| ≤ 1` and `|cx + d| ≤ 1`, so `c`
   and then `d` lie in a box `[−N, N] × [−M, M]` depending only on `τ`. Only finitely many
   bottom rows `(c, d)` can therefore beat the identity.
2. **A maximum exists** (`exists_max_im`). Minimising `|cτ + d|²` over the finite list of
   pairs in the box that occur as bottom rows (`list_argmin`) gives `γ₀` with
   `Im (γτ) ≤ Im (γ₀τ)` for **every** `γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ)`.
3. **Translate** by `T⁻ᵐ`, `m = ⌊Re(γ₀τ) + 1/2⌋`, to get `|Re| ≤ 1/2`; the imaginary part,
   and hence maximality, is unchanged.
4. **Invert.** If the result `τ'` had `|τ'| < 1`, then `Im (Sτ') = Im τ' / |τ'|² > Im τ'`
   would contradict maximality. So `|τ'| ≥ 1` and `τ' ∈ F`.

The conditions are stated with the squared modulus `|τ|² = normSq τ` (`|τ| ≥ 1 ⟺ |τ|² ≥ 1`,
`one_le_cabs_iff`). The uniqueness half (two interior points of `F` are equivalent only if
equal) is in `FundamentalDomainUnique`.

# Points of F have maximal height; interior points are inequivalent

The existence half of the fundamental-domain theorem (`FundamentalDomain`) moved every point
into `F = {|Re τ| ≤ 1/2, |τ| ≥ 1}`. This file proves the converse estimates.

* **Height is maximal on F** (`one_le_Q_of_mem_F`, `im_smul_le_of_mem_F`). For `τ = x + iy ∈ F`
  and any bottom row `(c, d) ≠ (0, 0)`,

    `|cτ + d|² = c²|τ|² + 2cdx + d² ≥ c² − |cd| + d² ≥ 1`,

  using `|τ| ≥ 1`, `|x| ≤ 1/2` and the integer inequality `c² ∓ cd + d² ≥ 1`
  (`int_quad_ge_one`). Hence `Im (γτ) ≤ Im τ` for every `γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ)`.

* **Interior points** (`eq_of_interior`). If `τ` and `γτ` both lie in the interior
  `|Re| < 1/2, |τ| > 1`, then both heights are maximal, so they agree and `|cτ + d|² = 1`.
  With strict inequalities this forces `c = 0`; then `γ = ±T^b`, so `γτ = τ + n` with
  `|n| < 1`, i.e. `γτ = τ`.

So the interior of `F` maps injectively to the orbit space `SL₂(ℤ)\ℍ`. (The identifications
on the boundary — `τ ↦ τ + 1` on the vertical sides and `τ ↦ −1/τ` on the arc — and the
stabilisers of `i` and `ρ = e^{2πi/3}` are not treated here.)

# S and T generate SL₂(ℤ)

The two transformations `S : τ ↦ −1/τ` and `T : τ ↦ τ + 1` generate the modular group. In
the language of quadratic forms this is Gauss's reduction; in matrices it is nothing but the
**Euclidean algorithm** applied to the first column `(a, c)`. Indeed, left multiplication by
`Tⁿ` replaces the top row by `top + n · bottom`, and left multiplication by `S` swaps the
rows up to sign. Dividing `a = qc + r` with `0 ≤ r < |c|` and multiplying by `S T⁻q` turns a
matrix with bottom-left entry `c` into one with bottom-left entry `r`. Since `|c|` strictly
decreases, after finitely many steps `c = 0`; then `ad = 1`, so the matrix is `±Tᵇ`, and
`−I = S²`.

We formalise "generated by" as an inductive predicate `Gen` (the smallest set containing
`S`, `T`, `1` and closed under products and inverses), package it as a `Subgroup`
(`genST`), show it is contained in every subgroup containing `S` and `T` (`genST_le`), and
prove `Gen g` for every `g` (`generation`). This is the "easier" Euclidean route; the
alternative derivation from the fundamental domain is not given.

Klein used generation by `S` and `T` to read off the shape of the modular figure, and it is
what makes the definition of a modular form checkable: a function satisfying the
transformation law for `S` and for `T` satisfies it for all of SL₂(ℤ) (file `Forms`).

# The transformation law of modular forms

A **modular form of weight `k`** for SL₂(ℤ) is a function `f : ℍ → ℂ` such that

  `f(γτ) = (cτ + d)^k f(τ)`  for all `γ = (a b; c d) ∈ SL₂(ℤ)`,

which is moreover **holomorphic** on ℍ and **holomorphic at the cusp** `i∞` (bounded as
`Im τ → ∞`). Eisenstein (1847) and Weierstrass gave the first examples, the series
`G_k(τ) = Σ' (mτ + n)^{−k}` for even `k ≥ 4`; Klein's `j`-invariant (1878) is the basic
modular *function* (weight `0`, meromorphic), and it classifies elliptic curves over ℂ up to
isomorphism. Hecke (1930s) attached `L`-functions with Euler products and functional
equations to modular forms, and this is the bridge to arithmetic.

**What is, and is not, formalised here.** The library has the complex numbers and some real
analysis, but no theory of holomorphic functions of a complex variable (no complex
derivative on open subsets of ℂ, no Laurent or `q`-expansions). We therefore define only the
**transformation law** `IsModular k f`, i.e. "weakly modular of weight `k`" with no
analytic condition. This is a predicate on arbitrary functions; it is *not* the notion of a
modular form, and nothing below is a modular form in the classical sense.

What we prove:

* the transformation law is consistent, thanks to the cocycle identity `denom_mul`;
* **it suffices to check `S` and `T`** (`isModular_of_S_T`): if `f(−1/τ) = τ^k f(τ)` and
  `f(τ + 1) = f(τ)`, then `f` satisfies the law for every `γ`, by generation (`Generation`);
* **odd weights are empty** (`eq_zero_of_odd`): `−I` gives `f = (−1)^k f`;
* **a non-trivial weight-0 example** (`height`): the *height* `h(τ) = max_γ Im(γτ)`, which
  exists by `FundamentalDomain.exists_max_im`, is SL₂(ℤ)-invariant (`height_smul`), equals
  `Im τ` on `F` (`height_of_mem_F`), and is not constant (`height_i`, `height_two_i`); hence
  `i` and `2i` are not equivalent (`not_equiv_i_two_i`). The height is a weight-0 invariant
  (its continuity is not proved here, and it is not holomorphic), not a modular function such as `j`.

## The modularity theorem and the automorphic side of Langlands (prose only)

Modular forms of weight `2` for the congruence subgroups `Γ₀(N) ⊂ SL₂(ℤ)` that are Hecke
eigenforms have Fourier coefficients `a_p` which are algebraic integers. The
**modularity theorem** (Wiles and Taylor–Wiles 1995 for semistable curves;
Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor 2001 in general) says that for every elliptic curve `E` over ℚ of conductor `N` there is such a
newform `f` with `a_p(f) = p + 1 − #E(𝔽_p)` for all primes `p ∤ N`. It implies Fermat's Last
Theorem via Frey, Serre and Ribet. **It is not stated or proved in this library.**

In Langlands' language a modular eigenform generates an *automorphic representation* of
`GL₂` over the adèles of ℚ, and an elliptic curve gives a two-dimensional *Galois
representation* (on its Tate module); modularity is the statement that these match prime by
prime, a case of the Langlands reciprocity conjecture for `GL₂`. The `Cyclotomic` chapter
treats the `GL₁` prototype on the Galois side; this chapter takes only the first step on the
automorphic side: the group, its action on ℍ, the fundamental domain, generation, and the
transformation law.

# Finite sums over squares of the lattice ℤ²

An Eisenstein series `Σ' (mτ + n)^{−k}` runs over the lattice `ℤ²`, which has no natural order.
We sum it over the **growing squares** `Q_N = {(m, n) : |m| ≤ N, |n| ≤ N}`, and this file
provides the finite combinatorics needed for that:

* interval sums `Σ_{a ≤ n < a + ℓ} h(n)` (`isum`) and square sums `Σ_{Q_N} g` (`sq`), built
  from the generic finite sums `gsum` of Part II;
* **embedding** a short interval into a longer one, padding with zeros (`isum_embed`), and
  its two-dimensional form, the **restriction** of a square sum to a smaller square
  (`sq_restrict`);
* the two **finite symmetries** of a square, `(m, n) ↦ (n, m)` (`sq_swap`) and
  `n ↦ −n` (`sq_neg_snd`), which are all the reindexing that the law under `τ ↦ −1/τ` needs;
* the **triangle inequality** for square sums (`cabs_sq_le`) and monotonicity of real ones;
* the **comparison lemma** `cabs_sq_ite_sub_le`, which is the heart of the rearrangement
  argument: if a finite region `P ⊆ Q_L` contains `Q_M`, then `Σ_P g` differs from `Σ_{Q_M} g` by
  at most `Σ_{Q_L} |g| − Σ_{Q_M} |g|`. When `Σ |g|` converges along squares, this difference is a
  tail and tends to zero; so any reasonable exhaustion of ℤ² gives the same sum;
* the **shell estimate** `sq_cabs_le`: counting the `8N` lattice points with `max(|m|, |n|) = N`,
  a bound `|g(m, n)| · max(|m|, |n|)³ ≤ B` gives `Σ_{Q_N} |g| ≤ 16 B` for every `N`;
* limits of complex sequences in the modulus (`CLim`), with uniqueness and the Cauchy criterion.

# The lattice-sum estimate

For `τ ∈ ℍ` the numbers `mτ + n`, `(m, n) ∈ ℤ²`, form a **lattice** `Λ_τ = ℤτ + ℤ` in ℂ. Since
`τ` and `1` are linearly independent over ℝ, a lattice vector can only be short if both of its
coordinates are small. Quantitatively (`lattice_estimate`):

  **there is `C(τ) > 0` with `|mτ + n| ≥ C(τ) · max(|m|, |n|)` for all integers `m, n`.**

We prove it from an explicit inequality for the positive definite quadratic form
`|mτ + n|² = (mx + n)² + (my)²` (`τ = x + iy`): with `D = x² + y² + 1`,

  `y² (m² + n²) ≤ 4D · |mτ + n|²`  (`normSq_lin_ge`),

and `C(τ) = √(y²/4D)`.

Consequently, for `k ≥ 3`, the terms `|mτ + n|^{−k}` are at most `C^{−k} max(|m|, |n|)^{−3}`
(`cabs_eterm_mul_le`). On the boundary of the square `Q_N` there are exactly
`(2N + 1)² − (2N − 1)² = 8N` lattice points, all with `max(|m|, |n|) = N`; so the contribution of
that shell is at most `8N · C^{−k} N^{−3} = 8 C^{−k} N^{−2}`. Summing over shells
(`Lattice.sq_cabs_le`, with `Σ 1/N² ≤ 2` by telescoping) gives

  **`Σ_{(m,n) ∈ Q_N} |mτ + n|^{−k} ≤ 16 C(τ)^{−k}` for all `N`** (`abs_lattice_sum_bounded`),

so the double series `Σ' |mτ + n|^{−k}` **converges** along squares (`abs_lattice_sum_converges`).
This is the classical argument of Eisenstein (1847), who was the first to sum such double series
with care, and it is what makes the definition of the Eisenstein series in the next file possible.

We also set up limits of complex sequences in the modulus (`CLim`), with uniqueness and the
Cauchy criterion, built on the completeness of ℝ.

# Eisenstein series and their transformation law

For an integer `k ≥ 3` and `τ ∈ ℍ`, the **Eisenstein series** of weight `k` is

  `G_k(τ) = Σ'_{(m, n) ∈ ℤ²} (mτ + n)^{−k}`,

the prime meaning that `(0, 0)` is omitted. We define it as the limit of the partial sums over
the squares `Q_N = {|m|, |n| ≤ N}` (`partialG`, `G`), which exists because the double series
converges absolutely (`LatticeSum.abs_lattice_sum_converges`): the partial sums form a Cauchy
sequence (`exists_eisenstein_limit`).

We then prove the **weight-`k` transformation law** (`G_isModular`):

* `G_k(τ + 1) = G_k(τ)` (`G_T`). Here the substitution `(m, n) ↦ (m, m + n)` does **not**
  preserve the squares: it maps `Q_N` onto a parallelogram lying between `Q_{N/2}` and
  `Q_{2N}`. So a genuine **rearrangement** of the double series is needed, and it is justified
  by absolute convergence: by the comparison lemma `Lattice.cabs_sq_ite_sub_le`, the sum over
  the parallelogram differs from the sum over `Q_{N/2}` by at most a tail
  `Σ_{Q_{2N}} |·| − Σ_{Q_{N/2}} |·|` of the absolutely convergent series, which tends to zero
  (`sq_shear`, `partialG_T_close`).
* `G_k(−1/τ) = τ^k G_k(τ)` (`G_S`). From `m(−1/τ) + n = (nτ − m)/τ` each term is
  `τ^k (nτ − m)^{−k}`, and `(m, n) ↦ (n, −m)` is a rotation of the lattice which maps every
  square `Q_N` onto itself; so already the partial sums transform correctly (`partialG_S`).

Since `S` and `T` generate SL₂(ℤ) (`isModular_of_S_T`), `G_k` satisfies the weight-`k` law
`G_k(γτ) = (cτ + d)^k G_k(τ)` for all `γ`. (For odd `k` this forces `G_k = 0`, by
`eq_zero_of_odd`; the interesting weights are the even `k ≥ 4`.) Holomorphy, and the behaviour
at the cusp, are not formalised in this library, so we say that `G_k` *satisfies the weight-`k`
law*, not that it is a modular form. As a first corollary, `G_k(i) = 0` whenever
`k ≡ 2 (mod 4)` (`G_i_eq_zero`), since `i` is fixed by `S` and `i^k = −1`.

## History

Eisenstein (1847) introduced such double series in his "Genaue Untersuchung der unendlichen
Doppelproducte, aus welchen die elliptischen Functionen als Quotienten zusammengesetzt sind",
paying careful attention to the order of summation, precisely because for `k ≤ 2` the double
series is only conditionally convergent and its value depends on that order. Weierstrass then
made `G_4` and `G_6` the coefficients of his elliptic function `℘` with periods `1, τ`:
`℘'² = 4℘³ − g₂℘ − g₃` with `g₂ = 60 G_4` and `g₃ = 140 G_6` (not formalised here).

In the Langlands programme Eisenstein series are where the whole story began: Langlands' own
starting point (*On the Functional Equations Satisfied by Eisenstein Series*, 1960s) was the
analytic continuation of Eisenstein series for general reductive groups, which gives the
continuous spectrum of `L²(Γ\G)` and, via their constant terms, the first automorphic
`L`-functions. None of that theory is formalised here.

# The Eisenstein series are not identically zero

The transformation law alone is satisfied by the zero function, so `G_isModular` would be
empty if `G_k` vanished identically. This file shows that it does not: for every even `k ≥ 4`,

  **`G_k(9i) ≠ 0`** (`G_ne_zero`), indeed `Re G_k(9i) ≥ 2/9` (`re_G_ge`).

The idea is the one behind the classical limit `G_k(iy) → 2ζ(k)` as `y → ∞` (which we do not
prove): split the lattice sum at `τ = iy` into

* the row `m = 0`, which is `Σ_{0 < |n| ≤ N} n^{−k}`; for even `k` its terms are positive reals
  and the two terms `n = ±1` already give `2` (`re_row_ge_two`);
* the rest `m ≠ 0`, where `|miy + n|² = m²y² + n²` is at least `max(|m|, |n|)²` and at least `y²`,
  so `|miy + n|^{−k} · max(|m|, |n|)³ ≤ 1/y` (`rest_bound`) and, by the shell estimate, the
  whole rest has modulus at most `16/y` (`cabs_rest_le`).

At `y = 9` this leaves `Re ≥ 2 − 16/9 = 2/9` for every square partial sum, hence for the limit.
Combined with `G_i_eq_zero`, for `k ≡ 2 (mod 4)` (`k ≥ 6`) the function `G_k` is a non-zero
solution of the weight-`k` law that vanishes at `i` (`G_nonzero_but_vanishes_at_i`).

# Part XV, chapter 4: the modular group and the upper half-plane

The Langlands programme has two sides. The chapters `Padic`, `Rep` and `Cyclotomic` work on
the arithmetic (Galois) side. This chapter takes the first step on the **automorphic side**,
whose oldest and most concrete instance is the theory of modular forms: functions on the
upper half-plane `ℍ` transforming in a prescribed way under the modular group SL₂(ℤ).

## History

Klein (1877–1880) and Poincaré (1880–1884) made SL₂(ℤ) and its subgroups central to analysis.
Klein studied the **modular figure**, the tessellation of ℍ by the images of one curvilinear
triangle, and the elliptic modular function `j`; Poincaré recognised the Möbius action as the
isometries of the hyperbolic plane and built automorphic functions for every Fuchsian group
from fundamental polygons. Earlier, Gauss's reduction theory of binary quadratic forms (1801)
had been the same fundamental-domain theorem in other words. Eisenstein, Weierstrass and later
Hecke supplied modular forms with arithmetic content, Hecke attaching to them `L`-functions
with Euler products.

**Modularity theorem (prose only, not formalised or claimed).** Every elliptic curve over ℚ is
modular: its `L`-function is that of a weight-2 newform on `Γ₀(N)` (Wiles; Taylor–Wiles;
Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor). In Langlands' terms, the 2-dimensional Galois representation
of the curve corresponds to an automorphic representation of `GL₂`; this is one case of the
reciprocity conjecture, far beyond what is built here.

## What is proved

* `SL2`: **SL₂(ℤ) is a group** (`SL2Z.instGroup`); the generators `S = (0 −1; 1 0)` and
  `T = (1 1; 0 1)` satisfy **`S² = −I`** (`S_mul_S`) and **`(ST)³ = −I`** (`ST_cube`).
* `Action`: on `ℍ = {Im τ > 0}` (`UHP`), the Möbius map `γτ = (aτ + b)/(cτ + d)` satisfies
  **`Im(γτ) = Im τ / |cτ + d|²`** (`im_mob`, `im_mob_cabs`), defines a **group action**
  (`instMulAction`), with cocycle `j(γδ, τ) = j(γ, δτ) j(δ, τ)` (`denom_mul`), and **`−I` acts
  trivially** (`negOne_smul`).
* `FundamentalDomain`: with `F = {|Re τ| ≤ 1/2, |τ| ≥ 1}` (`InF`, stated with `|τ|²`;
  `one_le_cabs_iff`), **every point of ℍ is equivalent to a point of F** (`exists_mem_F`),
  by maximising `Im` over the orbit (`exists_max_im`, using that only finitely many bottom
  rows have `|cτ + d| ≤ 1`, `bounds`), translating by a power of `T` and inverting by `S`.
* `FundamentalDomainUnique`: points of `F` have maximal height in their orbit
  (`im_smul_le_of_mem_F`), and **two interior points of F are equivalent only if equal**
  (`eq_of_interior`).
* `Generation`: **S and T generate SL₂(ℤ)** (`generation`, `genST_eq_top`), by the Euclidean
  algorithm on the first column; with an induction principle (`induction_on`).
* `Forms`: the **weight-k transformation law** `IsModular k f` (a predicate only: no holomorphy,
  since the library has no complex analysis); **S and T suffice** (`isModular_of_S_T`); odd
  weights force `f = 0` (`eq_zero_of_odd`); and a **non-constant weight-0 invariant**, the
  height `max_γ Im(γτ)` (`heightC_isModular`), which also shows `i ≁ 2i`
  (`not_equiv_i_two_i`).
* `SquareSums`: finite sums over the squares `Q_N = {|m|, |n| ≤ N}` of ℤ², their symmetries
  (`sq_swap`, `sq_neg_snd`), restriction (`sq_restrict`), and the **comparison lemma**
  (`cabs_sq_ite_sub_le`) behind every rearrangement below; limits in ℂ (`CLim`, `exists_CLim`).
* `LatticeSum`: the **lattice-sum estimate** `|mτ + n| ≥ C(τ) max(|m|, |n|)`
  (`lattice_estimate`); counting the `8N` points on each shell (`shell_step`, `sq_cabs_le`),
  **`Σ' |mτ + n|^{−k}` converges along squares for `k ≥ 3`** (`abs_lattice_sum_converges`).
* `Eisenstein`: the **Eisenstein series** `G_k(τ) = Σ' (mτ + n)^{−k}` (Eisenstein 1847), as the
  limit of square partial sums (`G`, `tendsto_G`); **`G_k(τ + 1) = G_k(τ)`** (`G_T`, by a
  rearrangement justified by absolute convergence), **`G_k(−1/τ) = τ^k G_k(τ)`** (`G_S`), hence
  **`G_k` satisfies the weight-k law** (`G_isModular`), and **`G_k(i) = 0` for `k ≡ 2 (mod 4)`**
  (`G_i_eq_zero`).
* `EisensteinNonzero`: **`G_k(9i) ≠ 0` for every even `k ≥ 4`** (`G_ne_zero`, via
  `Re G_k(9i) ≥ 2/9`), so the weight-k law has non-zero solutions in every even weight `≥ 4`
  (`G_nonzero_but_vanishes_at_i` for `k ≡ 2 mod 4`).

Eisenstein series are where Langlands himself started: his work on their analytic continuation
and functional equations for general groups produced the continuous spectrum and the first
automorphic `L`-functions (prose only; not formalised).

# Binary quadratic forms and the action of SL₂(ℤ)

A **binary quadratic form** is a homogeneous polynomial `f(x, y) = ax² + bxy + cy²` with
integer coefficients, written `f = (a, b, c)`. The question which integers such a form
represents is as old as Fermat's statement that an odd prime is a sum of two squares exactly
when it is `1 mod 4`. **Lagrange** (*Recherches d'arithmétique*, 1773–1775) found the key idea:
an invertible integral change of variables does not change the set of represented numbers, so
forms should be studied up to such substitutions, and every class contains a *reduced* form
with small coefficients. **Gauss**, in the fifth section of the *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae*
(1801), made this the centre of a whole theory: he distinguished *proper* equivalence
(substitutions of determinant `+1`), counted the classes of each discriminant — the
**class number** — and composed classes into what we now call the class group.

This file sets up the objects.

* `Form` is a triple `(a, b, c)`; `Form.eval` evaluates it and `Form.disc` is the
  **discriminant** `D = b² − 4ac`.
* A matrix `γ = (p q; r s) ∈ SL₂(ℤ)` acts by substitution, `(f·γ)(x, y) = f(px + qy, rx + sy)`
  (`Form.act`, `eval_act`). This is a right action: `f·I = f` and `(f·γ)·δ = f·(γδ)`
  (`act_one`, `act_mul`); turned into a left action by `γ • f = f·γ⁻¹` it is a **group action**
  in the sense of `Foundations.Algebra.MulAction` (`instMulAction`).
* The substitution **preserves the discriminant** (`disc_act`), because `D` gets multiplied by
  `(ps − qr)² = 1`, and **preserves primitivity**, i.e. `gcd(a, b, c)` (`content_act`).
* **Proper equivalence** `Equiv f g` is the orbit relation; it is an equivalence relation
  (`Equiv.refl`, `Equiv.symm`, `Equiv.trans`) and coincides with the orbits of the left action
  (`equiv_iff_orbit`).

The modular group used here is the from-scratch `SL2Z` of `Langlands.Modular.SL2`, the same
group that acts on the upper half-plane; the file `Reduction` explains the dictionary.

# Gauss reduction of positive definite forms

A form `f = (a, b, c)` with negative discriminant `D = b² − 4ac < 0` and `a > 0` is
**positive definite**: it takes only positive values away from `(0, 0)`. Lagrange (1773)
showed that each such form can be moved by substitutions into one with `|b| ≤ a ≤ c`; Gauss
(*Disquisitiones*, art. 171–172) sharpened the normalisation so that every class contains
**exactly one** reduced form:

  `f` is **reduced** iff `|b| ≤ a ≤ c`, and `b ≥ 0` whenever `|b| = a` or `a = c`.

## The algorithm (`exists_reduced`)

Two substitutions suffice, and they are the same two that generate `SL₂(ℤ)`:

* the translation `Tⁿ = (1 n; 0 1)` sends `(a, b, c)` to `(a, b + 2an, an² + bn + c)`
  (`act_Tn`), so `b` can be moved into the window `−a < b ≤ a`;
* the inversion `S = (0 −1; 1 0)` sends `(a, b, c)` to `(c, −b, a)` (`act_S`), swapping the
  outer coefficients.

If after translating `a > c`, swap with `S`: the new leading coefficient `c` is a smaller
positive integer, so the process terminates (strong induction on `a`). If `a ≤ c`, the form is
reduced except possibly when `a = c` and `b < 0`, which one more `S` repairs.

## The dictionary with the fundamental domain

To a positive definite form attach its root `τ_f = (−b + i√|D|)/(2a)` in the upper
half-plane ℍ, the zero of `f(τ, 1)`. Substitution of forms corresponds to the Möbius action
on roots, `|Re τ_f| = |b|/(2a)` and `|τ_f|² = c/a`, so `f` is reduced exactly when `τ_f` lies
in the fundamental domain `F = {|Re τ| ≤ 1/2, |τ| ≥ 1}` of `Langlands.Modular.FundamentalDomain`
(with the boundary conventions above choosing the left half of the boundary). The theorem
`exists_mem_F` there is thus the analytic form of the theorem proved here; we prove the
arithmetic version directly, without square roots, and do not formalise the root map.

# Uniqueness of the reduced form

Gauss's normalisation is chosen so that reduction is not only possible but **canonical**:
two different reduced forms of negative discriminant are never properly equivalent
(*Disquisitiones*, art. 172; in the modern form due to Dirichlet and Dedekind). On the
automorphic side this is the statement that the closed fundamental domain `F`, with its
boundary identified correctly, meets each orbit exactly once; the library file
`FundamentalDomainUnique` proves the interior case of that statement (`eq_of_interior`). Here
the **full** arithmetic statement is proved, boundary cases included, without the root map.

## The argument

For a reduced form `f = (a, b, c)` the smallest values are visible from the coefficients
(`le_eval`, `eval_ge_of_ne`):

* `f(x, 0) = ax² ≥ a` and `f(0, y) = cy² ≥ c ≥ a`;
* if `x, y ≠ 0` then `f(x, y) ≥ a − |b| + c ≥ c` (`core_bound`: for `x ≥ y ≥ 1` the difference
  is `(x − y)(ax + (a − |b|)y) + (a − |b| + c)(y² − 1) + (b + |b|)xy ≥ 0`).

So `a` is the minimum of `f` on `ℤ² ∖ {0}`. If `g = f·γ` with `γ = (p q; r s)`, then
`g.a = f(p, r)`; comparing minima in both directions gives `g.a = f.a`. Now two cases:

* `r = 0`: then `γ = ±(1 q; 0 1)` and `g.b = f.b ± 2aq`. Both middle coefficients lie in the
  window `−a < b ≤ a`, forcing `q = 0`, so `g = f`.
* `r ≠ 0`: the minimum `a` is attained at a point with non-zero second coordinate, which by the
  bounds above forces `c = a` (`c_eq_a_of_eval`); by symmetry also `g.c = g.a`. Then the
  discriminant gives `f.b² = g.b²`, and the boundary convention `b ≥ 0` when `a = c` gives
  `f.b = g.b`.

# Finiteness and class numbers

Reduction bounds the coefficients. If `f = (a, b, c)` is reduced with `D = b² − 4ac < 0`, then
`b² ≤ a² ≤ ac`, so

  `|D| = 4ac − b² ≥ 4a² − a² = 3a²`,  i.e. `a ≤ √(|D|/3)`  (`three_mul_sq_le`).

Given `D`, there are therefore only finitely many choices for `a`, then for `b` (`|b| ≤ a`),
and `c = (b² − D)/(4a)` is determined. Lagrange used exactly this to see that the number of
classes of each discriminant is finite; Gauss (*Disquisitiones*, art. 175 ff.) tabulated these
numbers. Following him we count **primitive** forms (`gcd(a, b, c) = 1`), since a
non-primitive form is an integer multiple of a form of smaller discriminant.

## What is defined and proved

* `candidates D` lists all triples `(a, b, (b² − D)/(4a))` with `0 ≤ 3a ≤ |D|`, `|b| ≤ a` — a
  crude but sufficient search space; `reducedForms D` keeps the reduced ones of discriminant
  `D`. For `D < 0` it contains **exactly** the reduced forms of discriminant `D`
  (`mem_reducedForms`) and has no repetitions (`reducedForms_nodup`).
* **Class number.** `classNumber D` is the number of primitive entries of `reducedForms D`.
  By `exists_reduced`, primitivity invariance (`content_act`) and `reduced_unique`, for
  `D < 0` the list `primReducedForms D` is a complete, irredundant system of representatives
  for proper equivalence classes of primitive positive definite forms of discriminant `D`
  (`primReducedForms_complete`, `primReducedForms_inequiv`), so `classNumber D` is the number of
  such classes.
* **Examples.** `h(−3) = 1`, `h(−4) = 1`, `h(−20) = 2`, `h(−23) = 3`, each with the explicit
  representatives and the class statements `classes_neg3`, `classes_neg4`, `classes_neg20`,
  `classes_neg23` (every positive definite form of that discriminant is equivalent to exactly
  one representative) (`reducedForms_neg20`: the classes of `x² + 5y²` and `2x² + 2xy + 3y²`;
  `reducedForms_neg23`: `x² + xy + 6y²` and `2x² ± xy + 3y²`). These are computed by `decide`
  in the kernel.

## Outlook (prose only)

Gauss composed classes of the same discriminant into a finite abelian group, the **class
group**, of order `h(D)`. Dirichlet's class number formula (1839) expresses `h(D)` through the
value at `s = 1` of an `L`-function; in the language of algebraic number theory, for
fundamental `D < 0` the class group of forms is the ideal class group of `ℚ(√D)`. Class field
theory (Hilbert, Takagi, Artin) identifies it with the Galois group of the **Hilbert class
field**, the maximal unramified abelian extension, and the primes represented by the principal
form are (apart from primes dividing `D`) those splitting completely there — e.g. for
`p ∤ 20`, `p = x² + 5y²` iff `p` splits completely in `ℚ(√−5, i)`. On the automorphic side,
reduced forms of discriminant `D` correspond to the CM points `τ_f ∈ F` of discriminant `D`,
and `j(τ_f)` generates the Hilbert class field (Kronecker's *Jugendtraum* for imaginary
quadratic fields). None of this is formalised here.


## Computed examples

# Which primes does a form represent?

Fermat claimed, and Euler proved, that an odd prime is `x² + y²` iff `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)`, is
`x² + 2y²` iff `p ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8)` and is `x² + 3y²` iff `p = 3` or `p ≡ 1 (mod 3)`. Euler
also conjectured that `x² + 5y²` behaves differently: the primes it represents should be
those `≡ 1, 9 (mod 20)`, while primes `≡ 3, 7 (mod 20)` are represented by
`2x² + 2xy + 3y²` instead. **Lagrange** (1773–1775) explained the pattern by the following criterion, which
reduces the question "which forms of discriminant `D` represent `p`" to a congruence.

## Results

* **Lagrange's criterion** (`prime_rep_iff`). For a prime `p` and any integer `D`:
  `p` is represented by some form of discriminant `D` iff `D` is a square modulo `4p`.
  (One direction completes a primitive representation `p = f(x, y)` to a matrix
  `γ = (x q; y s) ∈ SL₂(ℤ)` by Bézout, making `p` the leading coefficient of `f·γ`, so that
  `D = b'² − 4pc'`; the other writes down `(p, b, (b² − D)/(4p))`.) The usual statement has
  `p` odd, to rephrase the condition with a Legendre symbol; the version proved here needs no
  such hypothesis.
* **Applied to `x² + 5y²`.** If an odd prime `p ≠ 5` is `x² + 5y²` then `−20` is a square mod
  `4p` (`neg20_square_of_rep`), and by congruences mod 4 and mod 5,
  **`p ≡ 1 or 9 (mod 20)`** (`prime_x2_5y2_mod20`).
* **A converse, via the class number.** Since `h(−20) = 2`, a prime represented by some
  form of discriminant `−20` is represented by `x² + 5y²` or by `2x² + 2xy + 3y²`; odd values
  of the latter are `≡ 3 (mod 4)`. Hence **if `p ≡ 1, 9 (mod 20)` and `−20` is a square
  mod `4p`, then `p = x² + 5y²`** (`rep_x2_5y2_of_square`). The square condition itself follows
  from `p ≡ 1, 9 (mod 20)` by quadratic reciprocity; that step is not formalised here.

In the language of class field theory (prose only), for primes `p ∤ 20`: `p` is represented by *some* form of
discriminant `−20` iff `p` splits in `ℚ(√−5)`, and by the *principal* form iff it splits
completely in the Hilbert class field `ℚ(√−5, i)`, a condition that here happens to be a
congruence because the class group has exponent 2 (Gauss's genus theory).

# Part XV, chapter 5: binary quadratic forms, reduction and class numbers

This chapter is where the arithmetic side of the Langlands picture (integers, discriminants,
primes) meets the automorphic side (the modular group and its fundamental domain `F`).

## History

**Fermat** stated which primes are `x² + y²`, `x² + 2y²`, `x² + 3y²`; **Euler** proved these
and discovered that `x² + 5y²` needs a companion form. **Lagrange** (*Recherches
d'arithmétique*, 1773–1775) created the general theory: forms related by an invertible
integral substitution represent the same numbers, every form is equivalent to a *reduced* one,
there are finitely many reduced forms of each discriminant, and a prime `p` is represented by
some form of discriminant `D` exactly when `D` is a square modulo `4p`. **Gauss**, in section V
of the *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801), refined equivalence to *proper* equivalence
(determinant `+1`), fixed the reduction conditions so that the reduced form in each class is
unique, tabulated the **class numbers** `h(D)`, and introduced composition of forms, making the
classes a finite abelian group. Dirichlet (1839) found the analytic class number formula.

## The link with the fundamental domain

To a positive definite form `(a, b, c)` attach the root `τ = (−b + i√|D|)/(2a)` of `aτ² + bτ + c`
in the upper half-plane. Substitution of forms becomes the Möbius action of `SL₂(ℤ)`, and the
reduction conditions `|b| ≤ a ≤ c` say precisely `|Re τ| ≤ 1/2` and `|τ| ≥ 1`: Gauss's
reduction theory *is* the fundamental domain `F` of `Langlands.Modular.FundamentalDomain`
(Dedekind 1877, Klein 1879), the boundary conventions on `b` choosing one point from each pair
of identified boundary points. The library proves both theories independently; the root map
itself is described here in prose only.

## The link with class field theory (prose only)

For a fundamental discriminant `D < 0`, Gauss's class group is the ideal class group of
`ℚ(√D)`, and class field theory identifies it with the Galois group of the Hilbert class field
`H`. A prime `p ∤ D` is represented by the principal form iff it splits completely in `H`; values of
the modular function `j` at the roots `τ_f` generate `H` (complex multiplication). This is
the abelian (GL(1)) case of the reciprocity that Langlands generalises. Nothing in this
paragraph is formalised.

## What is proved

* `Basic`: forms `(a, b, c)`, the discriminant `b² − 4ac`; **SL₂(ℤ) acts by substitution**
  (`act_one`, `act_mul`, and as a left action `instMulAction`), **preserving the
  discriminant** (`disc_act`) and the content `gcd(a, b, c)` (`content_act`); proper
  equivalence `Equiv` is the orbit relation (`equiv_iff_orbit`), and equivalent forms
  represent the same integers (`Equiv.represents`).
* `Reduction`: **every positive definite form is properly equivalent to a reduced form**
  (`exists_reduced`), by the translation/inversion algorithm with strong induction on `a`.
* `Uniqueness`: a reduced form has minimum `a` on `ℤ² ∖ 0` (`le_eval`); **two properly
  equivalent reduced forms of negative discriminant are equal** (`reduced_unique`) — the
  full statement, boundary cases included; so each class has exactly one reduced form
  (`existsUnique_reduced`).
* `ClassNumber`: **`3a² ≤ |D|`** for reduced forms (`three_mul_sq_le`, i.e. `a ≤ √(|D|/3)`);
  the explicit duplicate-free list `reducedForms D` of all reduced forms of discriminant `D < 0`
  (`mem_reducedForms`, `reducedForms_nodup`); the **class number** `classNumber D`, the number
  of primitive reduced forms, with `classNumber_spec` showing it counts proper equivalence
  classes of primitive positive definite forms; and **`h(−3) = 1`, `h(−4) = 1`, `h(−20) = 2`,
  `h(−23) = 3`** (`classNumber_neg3`, …), with explicit representatives and the class
  statements `classes_neg3`, `classes_neg4`, `classes_neg20`, `classes_neg23`.
* `Representation`: **Lagrange's criterion** — a prime `p` is represented by some form of
  discriminant `D` iff `D` is a square mod `4p` (`prime_rep_iff`, for every prime `p`); for
  odd primes `p ≠ 5`, **`p = x² + 5y²` ⇒ `p ≡ 1, 9 (mod 20)`** (`prime_x2_5y2_mod20`); and,
  using `h(−20) = 2`, the converse **under the hypothesis that `−20` is a square mod `4p`**
  (`rep_x2_5y2_of_square`).

## Not formalised

The root map `f ↦ τ_f` and its equivariance; indefinite forms (`D > 0`), cycles of reduced
forms and Pell's equation; Gauss composition and the group structure on classes; genus theory;
the class number formula; the passage from `p ≡ 1, 9 (mod 20)` to "`−20` is a square mod `4p`"
(quadratic reciprocity, available elsewhere in the library but not connected here); ideal
classes, the Hilbert class field and complex multiplication.

# Part XV: Toward Langlands

The Langlands programme predicts a correspondence between Galois representations (arithmetic)
and automorphic representations (analysis), prime by prime and then globally. Nothing close to
that is formalised here. This part builds the first layers it stands on, from scratch:

* `Padic` — the local side at a prime `p`: the `p`-adic absolute value and the product formula,
  **Ostrowski's theorem** (every nontrivial absolute value on ℚ is equivalent to the usual one or
  to exactly one `|·|ₚ`), the `p`-adic integers `ℤₚ` (complete, compact), **Hensel's lemma**, `ℚₚ` as a complete
  field with `ℚ` dense, the Hilbert symbol at every place, and **Hilbert's product formula**
  for all nonzero rationals (`hilbert_product_formula`); **Legendre's theorem** and the
  **Hasse principle for conics** (`hasse_conic`, for admissible diagonal ternary forms).

* `Rep` — representations of finite groups, the language Langlands is written in: **Maschke's
  theorem**, **Schur's lemma** (with scalars over ℂ, via the fundamental theorem of algebra),
  characters and their **orthogonality**, multiplicities, and the bridge saying that for abelian
  groups the irreducible characters are exactly the Dirichlet-style characters of `DualGroup`; also complete reducibility, a complete list of irreducibles with
  Σ dim² = |G|, #irreducibles = #conjugacy classes, second orthogonality, characters determine
  representations, induced representations and Frobenius reciprocity, and the character tables
  of S₃ and A₄.

* `Cyclotomic` — reciprocity as Galois theory, the prototype of GL(1) reciprocity:
  irreducibility of `Φ_p` (Eisenstein), `Gal(ℚ(ζ_p)/ℚ) ≅ (ℤ/p)ˣ` (`cycloGaloisIso`), Gauss sums
  with `g² = p*`, **quadratic reciprocity re-proved by Frobenius** (`quadratic_reciprocity_gauss`,
  Gauss's sixth proof), and Dirichlet characters read as characters of the Galois group, with
  `χ(σ_q) = χ(q)` (`galChar_frobenius`), where `σ_q` is shown to be a Frobenius: it reduces
  to the `q`-th power map on `ℤ[ζ_p]` mod `q` (`reduce_galAut`). Also the degree `p − 1`, the
  quadratic subfield `ℚ(√p*)` as the fixed field of the squares, and, for **every** `n`,
  irreducibility of `Φ_n` (Dedekind's argument), `Gal(ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ) ≅ (ℤ/n)ˣ` (`cycloGaloisIsoN`),
  degree `φ(n)`, and the Frobenius congruence (`reduceN_galAut`); the **GL(1) dictionary**
  `dirichletGaloisN` between Dirichlet characters mod `n` and characters of `Gal(ℚ(ζ_n)/ℚ)`,
  matching at Frobenius and in finite unramified Euler products (`dirichletEuler_eq_artinEuler`).

* `Squares` — sums of squares: **Lagrange's four-square theorem**, the full two-squares
  characterisation, and **the three-square theorem** (n is a sum of three squares iff it is not
  4ᵃ(8b+7)), proved via Dirichlet's theorem, reciprocity, Legendre's theorem and
  Davenport–Cassels.
* `Modular` — the first step on the automorphic side: `SL₂(ℤ)` acting on the upper half-plane,
  the fundamental domain (every orbit meets it; interior points are inequivalent), generation by
  `S` and `T`, and the weight-`k` transformation law as a predicate (holomorphy is not
  formalised, so these are not yet modular forms); **Eisenstein series** `G_k` as absolutely
  convergent lattice sums satisfying the weight-`k` law (`G_isModular`), not identically zero for even `k ≥ 4` (`G_ne_zero`).

* `Forms` — binary quadratic forms: the `SL₂(ℤ)` action, **Gauss reduction** (every positive
  definite class has exactly one reduced form, `existsUnique_reduced`), the class number `h(D)`
  with `h(−3) = h(−4) = 1`, `h(−20) = 2`, `h(−23) = 3`, and which primes a form of discriminant
  `D` represents (`prime_rep_iff`); `p = x² + 5y²` forces `p ≡ 1, 9 mod 20`.

Not formalised: Hasse–Minkowski beyond conics, holomorphic modular forms (holomorphy of `G_k`, q-expansions, Δ, j), Kronecker–Weber, Artin reciprocity in general,
automorphic representations — that is, everything that makes Langlands Langlands.
Each sub-part's aggregator states exactly what it proves and what it does not.
